I would very much wish, Jakob Wimpfeling, that you would satisfy, even late at last, your promise and my expectation of you. You know, however, what you promised, and you are not ignorant of what I expect. I desire you not to be a monk, but to live with monks. Make haste, that we may live together. Behold, the hour of our passing, greatly to be feared, is at hand. Why then do we delay? Why, unhappy men, do we neglect the brief and wretched state of our [unclear]? Why do we refuse to do penance, in the time of salvation, for our transgressions and excesses? Let us prepare ourselves for death, since it hastens quite terribly, calls all the reprobate, spares no one, reveres no one; it denies audience to those who pray; it despises the tears of those who wail; it scorns the threats of princes, and destroys the names and glory of kings; it brings to nothing the hateful pride of tyrants before all. Therefore, brother, diligently considering the benefits of the Redeemer shown to us, very useful to us, let us repay them by amending our offenses, continually shining with good morals, so that by penance and tears we may be able to placate the strict examination of the judge hastening to the judgment seat, who will show himself terrible to the rejected, pleasant to the elect. Farewell from Sponheim, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord M.D.CW. When

Our Savior Jesus Christ, who, dying on the Cross, redeemed the human race by his blood, must be praised by us earnestly and without interruption. He himself will drive away death, and he has also promised that he will deliver eternal [life] to us who fear and love him. Now therefore let us rise up, dearest brothers, from our sins, setting our lamps in order with good works, so that we may joyfully meet the Redeemer in the hour of the fearful passage, when death will seize our souls. We now have abundant time for fulfilling penance and for adorning our lamps; but in the final hour of death the space for repenting further will be altogether denied us. Let us consider the very brief glory of the world, since it is vain: it passes away most swiftly, and we with it are corrupted every hour. Therefore let us humble our hearts at all times, never failing. In the year 1513, on the Kalends of April.

[unclear]

Buriel, Thresoy chamerontis, hayr plassu, nadiel, marso, neany, pean, sayr, fabelron, chaturmo, melros, ersoty caduberosyn. When the charm has been spoken, a spirit invisible to all, but visible to you, will appear, and let him faithfully speak the secret entrusted to him.

FIRST BOOK.

CHAPTER XXIII.

Whose spirit and supreme prince is called Hydriel, and dwells in waters, having under him 100 leaders, 200 companions, and almost innumerable servants.

[unclear]

There is another prince among the principal spirits, who is called Hydriel, and he dwells in waters, fishponds, lakes, marshes, and the sea, and around springs, cisterns, and rivers, having under his dominion at least 100 leaders or princes, and 200 companions or subordinate leaders, and many servants. Their office is generally to announce all things, both by waters and by land, whether it be by day or by night. And know that the princes are quite benevolent and willing in all things, but they do not appear so when they come after being conjured. For they frequently appear in the form of a serpent, sometimes large, sometimes small, having a very beautiful maiden’s head, with hair spread out. None of them goes alone, but each prince brings with him at least two companions and 80 servants. So that you may not fall into error in the operation, I shall set down for you the names of some of the leaders.

Mortaliel Lameniel Camiel 10 20 100 200 Chamoriel Brachiel Arhiel 10 20 100 200 Pesariel Samiel Lusiel 10 20 100 200 Musaziel Dusiriel Chariel 10 20 100 200 Behold, you have from the princes and leaders of Hydriel 12, and from the companions and servants 1320, who suffice for your operations in Steganography according to the order of the 24 hours, so that each leader has 2 hours, and the companions and servants 110 in their orders, which you must know completely. When, through these princes of spirits, you wish to do anything in Steganography, do what you know must be done according to the art, and say the conjuration.

Song.

Hydriel, apron chamerote, satrus pean nearmy chabelon, vearchas, belta, nothelmy phameron, arsoy pedaryn onzel, Lamedo drubel areon veatly cabyn noty maleros haytny pe fary does, pen rasi medusan ilcohi person. When the song has been spoken, the spirit whom you have called will be present, with the servants assigned to him according to the hour, and he will be obedient to you in all things, faithful for everything to which you send him.

X.

Let us imagine some secret matter.

Let there be for me some very secret matter of any sort whatever for a friend, which I cannot safely make known to him either by letters or by [messenger?]. Therefore, lest the secret come to light, I summon the spirit; he comes, he obeys; I entrust the secret; he carries it faithfully.

X.

Let us compose letters of any kind whatever.

Johannes Tritt., Abbot of Spanheim, sends greeting to Brother Peter Marponius Gisemius, laureate, a monk of the Rhine.

Brother Nicolaus, Bishop of Trbusium and suffragan of the most reverend father and most illustrious duke Adam of Insignisburg in Pantomorania, a most honorable and distinguished archprelate, an indefatigable lover of books, seems most justly to compare an abbot, Vinilianus by name, to beasts, because he is one who feasts splendidly among the dung-heaps of beasts and prefers calves to volumes, as Reuchlin has affirmed. I ask that you imitate Nicolaus, the best and most gentle bishop. Farewell, 21 March 1505.

When you have received these letters, or any others, with the sign of Hydriel, with no consideration of the sphere observed, but only after the general preliminaries that must be prefaced in the art have been put first, as customary say the following.

Conjuration.

Hydriel omar, penadon epyrma narsoy greol fabelrusin adiel pedrufij nozeui melrays vremy pean larfoy naes chemetyn.

When this conjuration has been spoken in the proper way, according to the instruction of the art, the spirit will appear to you visibly, revealing in your ear the secret entrusted to him.

CHAPTER XXIV.

Whose prince is called Pyrichiel, having under him many leaders, princes, companions, and servants, whose number is uncertain.

Pyrichiel, a certain supreme prince of spirits, seems to us to have to be wholly rejected from our art, because he is said to be quite benevolent. He does not have under him leaders or princes in the manner of the rest, but only companions and subordinate servants, whose number is uncertain. There are those who say that he has leaders and princes under him; they seem to us not to understand his property and custom well enough, since they have imagined companions and servants as leaders. The name of Pyrichiel derives its designation from fire, because he is frequently accustomed to be occupied around fire.

Let us posit any secret whatsoever.

Let there be for me a secret for a friend far absent, which I cannot safely send by letters, lest they be read when [unclear], or certainly [unclear] on the road. I have less confidence in a man to carry it, since I know that trustworthiness in men changes with fortune. Therefore, so that all things may be safe, I call upon the spirit, friend of the secret: he comes at once, having heard the song, and faithfully carries what has been entrusted to him.

Let us form the letters as one pleases.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Jacobus Dracomius, canon of the Premonstratensian order, greeting and charity.

There is with us a notable mathematician and excellent rhetorician, constantly devoted to the study of a most tranquil life. He has with him almost infinite books, and an inestimable treasure of diverse exemplars: a pleasant and kindly teacher of upright and honorable life and of honorable society; most experienced in resolving doubts. He explains great matters: his name is Orophanius, burgrave of the kingdom of Bosnia. Farewell, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

When the person to whom they are sent, skilled in the art of Steganography, has received these or any similar letters, signed with the character of Pyrichiel, let him do as he knows must be done according to the art; then, with a light lit, let him say this conjuration.

He has under his dominion 100 princes and dukes, no fewer than 20 counts or subdukes, and servants and slaves without any fixed number. From these we shall name some who may suffice for us in working, reserving the rest, with others, to be named in their place if there is need.

A secret, whatever sort you wish.

I have a friend who everywhere trusts all men too much, who cherishes enemies as friends, from whom he often receives both bad repute and harm. He is credulous toward the flatteries of those who fawn upon him, and especially of one man who clings to his side, whom he does not know to be opposed to him in secret, because he sees him to be ingratiating in public. I wish to accuse him, yet in such a way that the advice becomes known to the friend alone; to the rest it will be hidden.

Let the tenor of the letters be formed at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Reverend Father and Lord Nicolaus, Bishop of [Irbursiensis?], Vicar of the Archbishop of [Pantomoranus?], greeting.

D.P.

When I bring your talent and the uprightness of your life back to mind, Reverend and most excellent Father, I am especially compelled to pronounce you most worthy of all bishops. For indeed, whether one considers the learning in you of the good arts, or the innocence of your life, what else should I call you but most just, most learned in all letters, and to be revered for your morals? You adorn your conduct with works of rectitude, and always show yourself an excellent shepherd of souls; and in letters you continually exercise yourself by study, so that you may benefit yourself and others in both respects. Farewell. Given from Spanheim, 11 Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1501.

Chapter XXVI.

Whose supreme emperor is called Icosiel, having under him 100 dukes or princes, 300 counts or subdukes; the number of servants is not yet certain to me.

Icosiel, among the aerial spirits, is one of the more powerful, a great and powerful emperor in the secrets of Steganography, having under him 100 princes of ducal order. But counts, 300; I have not yet found the certain number of servants. He is called Icosiel for this reason, because he gladly spends time with men in houses. For afterward, when you have once duly conjured and called to yourself any one of his dukes with his counts, if you wish him to remain with you all the days of your life

Steganography 76 may remain: assign him one secret and hidden place in your house; once he has been strongly conjured, command him to remain there; he will obey you cheerfully, and will always be ready at your command.

Make the letters to be sent as you please. Let the secret be whatever you wish.

A friend of mine, far absent from me, is skilled in the art of Steganography; I have for him a great secret and hidden matter, which must not be entrusted to anyone, even by letters, nor even hinted at. Therefore, so that all things may remain secret, I send as secret messenger a Spirit, who is to reveal the secret to my friend and keep my business secret.

Let us amend our life, humbling ourselves before the highest maker of the universe. Humility obtains Heaven; it annihilates the harmful temptations of demons; it restrains the pernicious swelling of the mind, and powerfully exterminates all fires of vices. The path of humility deserves to receive a crown and to possess a noble kingdom. I establish for you as a path innocence and uprightness of conduct; by guarding it continually, you will not sin. This alone is the way for us to heap up the merit of blessedness: that, giving thanks to God, we fear him with a most upright heart, fleeing the tumult of the world; let us never grow weary of the exercise of humility, seeking the life above. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, writer, 10 Kalends of April, 1500.

I decide that a friend far absent, previously skilled in the art of Steganography, must be warned about certain imminent dangers. But I fear the public, since I would be making another’s danger my own; so that I may avoid this, I entrust the secret neither to letters nor to men, but to a spirit whom I know will be most faithful in all things.

Let us form letters at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, sends many greetings to the Reverend Father in God Rutger Sycamber, Archbishop of Narva.

The most reverend and most studious Nicolaus, bishop of Irburs, general governor of your ecclesiastical affairs, will explain to you that [unclear] has acted badly, by subjecting to bonds the vicar of our lord King Desiderius, a benign man, and has killed him, tormented by hunger. We are expecting the enemy Desiderius the king, breaking daily into the diocese. But we entreat you: come to aid shortly, so that you may not fall into the enemy. Farewell. 24 March 1503.

[unclear]

Although the things we have said seem to us to suffice abundantly for every operation of Steganography, nevertheless, lest we consign to oblivion those things which we have experienced, it has pleased us to add still some further matters, which, by the revelation of the aforesaid spirits, we have learned to be most excellent for the perfection of this art, and have experienced quite fully. Thus, among the other spirits who favor this art, there is one who has obtained the name Menadiel by reason of his office, who has under him twenty princes and leaders, one hundred counts, and many servants, whose number is uncertain to me; all of them are faithful in commissions and the best messengers in the great affairs of kings and princes, through whom we shall accomplish wonders.

Great and eternal are the things that will be for the advantage of those who observe innocence: for men rejoicing to be present at angelic praises; to behold that lofty light; the splendor of eternal blessedness, and to see the face of majesty by its own light. Pay attention, all of you, and wipe away past negligences with tears; put off useless cares and harmful ones; shudder, O muddy men, at the deceptions of unstable things; at last seek the profit of souls. Be honorable in good morals and virtues; despise vanities; humbly call upon God; do not desire the world, which pours in bitterness. In the year 1500, the ninth day before the Kalends of April. d-

Chapter XXIX.

Whose supreme prince is called Macariel, having under his command many dukes, princes, counts, and servants appointed to various services.

Macariel also, one of the supreme spirits who preside over the operations of Steganography, must not be omitted by us, together with his serving princes, because he is sufficiently useful, prompt, and faithful for all things whatsoever we may wish. He has forty princes; of these, never fewer than four are sent into service, namely three dukes and one count, with not a few servants. They observe this order among themselves, that in their turns one of the dukes always performs the office of count, according to the four parts of the year. And concerning all these it is necessary for the operator to have full knowledge. But now let us name some of the princes themselves, who will abundantly suffice us for the operation of our Steganography.

When this chant has been spoken, the spirits summoned will be present, appearing in diverse form, and often indeed with a virgin’s head, while their body and tail end in the form of a dragon, twisting and turning themselves in a fourfold order.

A secret matter is sent to the prince.

The prefect of the king or prince, appointed in a land or province, has understood by a most secret report that the enemies shortly have the intention of breaking into the province. He wishes to warn the prince, but he cannot do so by messengers, because they are to be tortured by the adversaries on the road so that they may betray the secret; nor by letters, since all letters are opened by them. Therefore he summons a spirit, entrusts the secret, and composes unrelated letters.

Let us compose letters conveying nothing.

We ask, sweetest of friends, that, in view of our old friendship, you would quickly send us your copy of Tertullian, the noblest and wisest man, so that it may be copied out for us: Bernard’s Epistle to the Templars.

To Tertullian, glorious in the Catholic name of sanctity, shown by all antiquity among our own: and noble, a light, we know that he did not remain last in the holy faith. In actions he was distinguished, a glorious teacher of the divine law, defender of our liberty, devo-

34 devoted to Steganography. Although he is criticized in some respects, nevertheless, in expounding our faith, he wrote honorable volumes. He had a jealous wife, a lover of our religion, noble in humility and innocence, glorious in chastity. There survive some praiseworthy lucubrations of his of right instruction, and many sweet and abundant teachings: short letters, not useless, honorably and graciously exhorting us to seek eternal glory. On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1500. Johannes Trithemius wrote this.

When you have received these letters, or any others whatever, he to whom they are sent, being beforehand skilled in the art of Steganography, once the sign of Macariel has been recognized, should do what is customarily to be done, adding the song.

In addition, one remains of the supreme Spirits, assigned to us for the operation of Steganography: last indeed in order, but among the first in dignity. His name, by reason of his office, is called Bydiel, having under his command 20 dukes, or 200 counts or sub-dukes, and many attendants and servants. These dukes, together with the counts, have a fixed order among themselves; and as often as they are called by the operator, two dukes come with 20 counts, and appear in human form, gentle and ready for all things. They alternate among themselves, so that when in the first year the dukes have been called, afterwards the counts are called; in the second year the counts are called in place of the dukes.

Let it be secret to me, whatever it may be.

It is a secret to me, which I desire to know, a very secret friend absent far away: it concerns a hidden substance, which must be lost if the mystery happens in any way to be made public. Therefore I entrust it to be carried not to a man, nor to letters, but to spirits alone, whom I know to be safe and faithful.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Rutger the Sicambrian. And let him say the following little prayer of great Basil.

The glory of ineffable eternal blessedness is acquired by good and humble exercises. Now, mortals, wipe away your errors with diligent tears: love God, adoring his holy name. Strive humbly to imitate the path of humble Jesus Christ, crucified, always rendering honor to him, sweetly burning with love of our most benign Savior. Glorify, exalt his praiseworthy goodness; bless the holy name, zealously pursuing the fire of goodness. Despise empty honors; learn to render praises in adversities; love the exercise of devotion; cultivate humility, the most noble thing; exalt Jesus, rescuing and saving us from death. Farewell. 7 days before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1500.

The First Book.

…[the secrets] of wisdom, nor does nature help, when they have not been able to understand this most secret art of our invention—[this] is not to be imputed to us, but rather they will understand it is to be ascribed to their own sloth, laziness, and malice: namely those who, having their wit immersed in the pleasures of the flesh and worldly cares, cannot with diligence be at leisure to survey these things; or who, deeming themselves already wise or most learned, despise our compositions as unworthy of their reading. There will be also some so accustomed to rest in old and alien traditions that they deem whatever they have not learned in them either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more inept for the knowledge of this profound art than these, who either will not or cannot contemplate its loftiest [matters]. But those who are both apt and willing to study in this art (if any there shall be)—that they may be able to make progress—we have determined to admonish in a few [words] at the end of this book. First of all they are to be admonished that they always keep the art itself hidden, lest it penetrate the hand and notice of the wicked, who would do many and execrable crimes through it. For although the art itself is truly good in itself, yet its practice would conduce no less to evil through the impious than to good through the good. Let the secret therefore remain among the good, which, published among the wicked, would do harm. Nor, however, ought the good to despise this knowledge because it profits the wicked unto evil; just as he who lays a man low does not spurn the sword. Then the studious of this art are to be admonished not to presume to proceed to operating in it, unless first they have been perfectly instructed in all [things] which are required for the practical science. For it does not escape me to how great dangers they subject the matter who, less skilled, have at any time attempted to operate something in it. Likewise, whoever, well instructed in this science, shall wish to operate through it, let him remember to observe diligently (according to those [things] which we have said, as much in the circle as in the individual tables and chapters) the difference, the places, names, orders, and offices of the supreme Spirits, their dukes also, and how many counts there are in number; which order let him obser[ve]… observe, and who are placed over the substitutes, so that he may know how to express these things in the conjuration. For unless the practitioner of the art has carefully observed all these things, he will not be able to make progress, nor to arrive at the effect of his intention. Again, let him attend carefully when each spirit is to be called for which duties or secrets, and in what quarter of the world he dwells, lest he err either in the places or in the [names?] of the several ones whom he wishes to call.

Likewise, let everyone who is to operate in this science be advised to attend most diligently to pronouncing the words of the conjurations properly, for in them lies the great force of our operation; since, when an error is committed in the conjurations, the spirits called, or to be called, not only do not obey, but even wholly resist. Consequently, let him also be forewarned not to call one for another, but each one in his own order, time, and office, just as has been sufficiently stated by us in nearly all the chapters of this book. For if, either through error or through any other negligence, he calls one for another, he will make no progress in his operation, but will bring danger upon himself.

Likewise, in the conjurations the spirit who is called should be expressed by name together with his substitutes; the cause of the calling should first be fixed in the intention; nor should the act of operation be performed in light, profane matters, which one person can otherwise communicate safely to another without danger, whether by letters or by messengers. For this art is to be used only for announcing great and difficult matters which, if made public, would bring loss or danger upon the operator. Likewise, it is necessary for everyone operating in this art to know the natures of the spirits: which are good, which evil, which ready and well-disposed to obedience, which harsh and rebellious. Again, which preside over nocturnal operations, and which over diurnal ones; because unless he has known the natures of the spirits before he begins to operate, he will make progress with the greatest difficulty and will easily be turned to stupor. Likewise, when the spirits called appear visibly before the operator, after the secret word has been sent ahead, let him entrust the secret of his mind to the duke or count in appropriate words, under silence; for there is no need to speak to the spirit in a raised voice, but let him use a low one.

Care must also be taken with the greatest diligence, both by the operator and by the recipient, that they do not perform anything pertaining to Steganography in the presence of other men ignorant of this art, when they can have access to a secret place. But if they cannot be alone, and it happens that they are compelled to operate among others, let them act so secretly, so prudently, and with such industry that none of those sitting around understands anything about the presence of the spirits. For all the spirits assigned to the ministry of this art are of such a nature and condition that they utterly detest and flee the tumult of men, and hate a public gathering. Likewise, the operator must also take care not to direct any spirit anywhere without letters, or at least without the character of his emperor; for when he does not see that very character impressed, he utterly refuses to obey the one calling him and to carry the secret to anyone. We send letters for a twofold reason, although we could announce the secret without letters through the spirit alone: namely, so that we may preserve from suspicion the men carrying the character, and so that, by that very character, we may constrain the spirit bound to obey the friend.

Here ends the first book of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, 27 March, 1500 [unclear].

Here Begins the Second Book of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, Archsteward of the Holy Empire and Prince Elector.

Preface.

In the preceding book, relying on the help of the highest God, we arranged in order, not without great labor, the thirty-one supreme spirits, emperors of our art, together with their dukes, counts, and servants necessary for us in operation. Although their ministries are abundantly sufficient for every operator for the announcement of all secrets, however secret, still, lest we seem to omit anything that can conduce to the perfection of this art, we have resolved to join a second book to the first. Since, moreover, by the tradition of certain wise men, individual spirits have been assigned to the individual hours of day and night for various operations and diverse and wondrous effects, it has pleased us to imitate only their order, not their superstition, so that, without injury to the Christian name, we may take from them what conduces to our purpose; but the rest, as being full of magical arts and contrary to our faith,

Preface.

[unclear] let us pass through by laying low [unclear]. Therefore, taking up, for each single hour both of day and of night, the principal spirits appointed by the secret of Solomon, surnamed Hermes, in his volume On Magic, as the supreme emperors of the art, together with the other officials necessary to us for the operation proposed, we shall proceed; and we shall give both method and instruction to all students in this art, by which at any hour they may disclose the secret and hidden conception of their minds to friends with safer counsel. For each prince presides like a watchman over his spirits, dukes, counts, and servants; at his command, when summoned by us with a lawful song, they come; they carry the entrusted secrets, and show themselves obedient and ready for us in all things. But since I am going to mention spirits again, I think I must preface once more: nothing in this art of ours is held to be frivolous; nothing contrary to evangelical tradition or the Catholic faith; nothing at all superstitious is handed down. For everything that we have said in the preceding volume, or shall say in those that follow, is supported by natural, lawful, and honorable principles; and the mystery veiled only by foreign institutions, and words wrapped in the names of spirits, require a learned reader. For we use the service of a spirit to veil a secret which, if published, would harm the reprobate. And lest anyone fail through error in the reckoning of the hours, let him know that we have accepted the hours of the planets both by day and by night.

Chapter.

Chapter I.

Samael, supreme emperor, presides over the first hour of the day; he has under his command many dukes, counts, and servants, whom, when called in this hour only, he sends to one experienced in working in Steganography.

The emperor-spirit of the first hour of the day, which takes its beginning at sunrise, is called Samael. He has under his command many dukes, counts, and subordinate servants; when summoned by the operator in this hour only, in Steganography, they come. They carry the secret that is entrusted to them, but they utterly refuse to come outside the hour. And note that Samael's first dukes, the princes, are rarely sent by him into the service of this science, since they hold office in stirring up men's magical nocturnal illusions. But the counts, with their attendants, have been specially appointed to the service of this art; into this they are also more often sent without the presence of the dukes. Since they are from the highest order among spirits, they are accustomed to show themselves somewhat proud and rebellious to those who summon them, nor do they easily obey anyone, unless he is most skilled in the art of Steganography, without labor and danger. For they are impudent, very ready for illusions and mockeries of men, and they especially deride and jeer at those whom they find to be less skilled in the art of Steganography. But those whom they consider bold, steadfast, and experienced in that art, they respect and fear, and they always obey their commands most promptly, with trembling reverence. And so now we shall report the names of those counts who are necessary to us in the operations of Steganography in this hour.

We now have, from the dukes of great Samael, four, and from the counts the same number; from the servants, from the threefold order, 4,440, whose ministry is abundantly sufficient for us for every operation of the art of Steganography, with respect to the first hour of the day.

Therefore, when you wish to operate in the art in the first hour, write first on a slip the character of the lord of the ascendant, then that of the moon; afterward those of all the remaining planets according to the customary order, and at the end the character of the sign ascending at that same hour. And when you have completed this, write on the back of the same slip this conjuration in silence, keeping silent:

Conjuration.

Samael afluar onayr myscolayar madiel cuhiel naniel nabruys satiel atharbiel nadian naslon, ranyalcoha pemarson.

When this conjuration has been written on the slip, as stated above, you will fit the letters to be sent, neatly, clearly, and distinctly, to him whom you wish to know the secret, in whatever form pleases you; for it makes no difference how the letters to be sent have been shaped, provided that they contain no secret in themselves. Then, once the letters too have been written, call one or two of the counts according to the order, if you are operating many times in this same first hour of the day, and say the conjuration prescribed from the same slip, with the strongest intention, fearing nothing. When it has been duly completed, the spirits called will immediately appear to you, visible, in a familiar form customary to themselves, peaceful, well-disposed, most ready for all services that arise. When they appear, entrust your secret to the chief one among them, saying: Ameniel, by the hidden power of this conjuration I command you to go as quickly as possible to Albert Goeler of Ravensburg, prefect in Kreuznach, and to tell him in my name thus or thus. When these words have been said, add the secret word, which must not be written; and immediately the spirit will fly away. Send the letters, sealed with the character of Samael, as is customary, by a messenger; let them contain no secret and fear no one’s inspection.

The secret is whatever occurs.

[unclear]

Let the secret be a great and difficult secret, whatever occurs at the time, and such that it ought to be communicated to no one, nor entrusted to letters or to messengers; for in this art, especially through the spirits of this second volume, one must not operate for small and trivial causes, which can otherwise be announced by letters.

You will compose letters on these matters at will.

The majesty of the Catholic faith, to be firmly preserved by all men, has promised ease of eternal life to those serving Christ. Hold the Catholic Christian faith; glorify the Almighty, fleeing the tumult of vanity. No one of depraved works will have the blessed life. Let the faithful man follow Christ in the path of virtues. Integrity is adorned by good works, and the Catholic name is preserved by Christian fidelity. For a depraved man darkens faith. Christ hates the rash, and loves Christians practicing Catholic works, venerating tranquillity. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, published this on the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1500[unclear].

When you have received the letters, let the person to whom they are sent, skilled in the art, first set forth those things that must be set forth from the general instruction of the art, and let him say the prescribed conjuration in that manner and rite in which we have said above that it was written on the slip, with the character of the lord of the ascendant and the other things expressed. But as soon as he has completed the conjuration, he will see the spirit present; when he has seen him, let him say fearlessly: + penador auenal + folmeniel phanu + fauear caschanti hernoty maduran. Amen. When these words have been said, let him be silent, and he will see the spirit approaching him and reporting the entrusted secret secretly and securely into his ear. Let him listen to him thus without fear and with great diligence, so that if anyone is sitting around him, he may not indicate by nod or word that the spirit is present.

The tenor of the letters is made familiar.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Wilhelm Veldicus, canon of Saint Augustine in the valley of Franconia, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

I would rejoice to answer your letter, so may Christ make me rejoice, and I would send the volumes requested, if at last I had them. For I have been zealous with a good zeal, such as the most ancient philosophers had, for the greatest and weightiest hidden treatises of nature. Moreover, I owe you truly immortal thanks, my sweetest brother, who have kept the bond of mutual exchange unbroken. For this fami-

Book Two.

... in a familiar matter, which you seem to have managed most diligently with grave modesty, I have plainly understood; this deed I praise, and I give thanks that will never die. And so I would very much wish to comply with your requests, if I had the things asked for, Christ knows. I have lately seen various Latin translations of [Ficiatus?]; I have read many most brilliant volumes of Pico della Mirandola, a most excellent man. I have seen Hippolytus in Greek; whether he has been completely translated, I do not know. The highest Truth, Christ, knows, from whom no darkness hides anything, that from my heart I wish to comply with you when you ask. I beg you, with zeal for virtue and zeal for rectitude: despise praises and honors that will perish. Consider true praise to be the imitation of Christ, who goes before. See to it, I beg, that you are a priest in works, and that you love Christ throughout all the time in which you live. The true rest of the soul, and pious knowledge of the Savior, observance of Catholic tradition, [unclear] eternal glory prescribed for all. May Jesus Christ, the glorious giver of all good things, confer on you Catholic love of eternity, making you a priest of Christians. Farewell. 4 Kalends of April, in the year 1500.

When the person to whom the letters have been sent has received them, being skilled in the art, after the customary preliminaries have first been set forth in general, let him arrange the lord of the ascendant with the other things that are customary on the chart, and let him say the prescribed conjuration. Once it has been said, the spirit sent will appear visibly; turning to him, let him say fearlessly: Fabelmerufyn passoriel liertos ryneas melchus thyrmo nydran year padroys. When this song has been completed, the spirit will at once approach gently and will faithfully disclose the mystery entrusted to him. But everyone who is to work in this art should beware, both he who sends the spirit and he to whom it has been directed, lest they presume to perform anything in public or among others who are not skilled in this art; because all hourly spirits love secrecy and detest publicity, and they would not depart without danger.

You Will Form Letters at Will.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Arnoldus Bostius, Carmelite of Ghent, fellow philosopher: greeting and charity.

Since I have known you to be a lover of the humane arts, and a devout [unclear] of the Christian faith, and the greatest supporter of all philosophers, I gladly comply with your requests, moved by the wondrous pleasure of friendship. Behold, at your urging I send you the book on writers, marked beforehand with ecclesiastical and Catholic doctors, so that you may have something with which to delight your mind. But send back to me the codex of Hermes, the books of Dionysius on spirits, and the great work of Euencius on winter questions. May Christ deign to adorn the eyes of our heart with the most fervent zeal of his love; and may he make us have love of heavenly goods; and, having stripped us of the basest desires, may he teach us to despise vain honors, so that we may be able to penetrate the sublime things of the art, and also the great secrets of nature; and may we have a continual desire for philosophy, to purify our affections, so that we may always adorn the Catholic faith with the most honorable morals. Hold fast the great word: you are a philosopher; give up everything, and you will find it. Keep watch for the hour of your approaching death, so that you may meet it prepared. Farewell. 3 Kal. Apr. 1500.

John Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Rutger Vencaius the Sicambrian, canon of the order of the divine father Augustine of the monastery of Dameten, greeting.

Those matters which you proposed to me to be resolved, with Christ’s help, I have resolved. Whether well, you who proposed them shall pronounce judgment. I shall briefly report to you an astonishing event that took place. A certain brother recently reported to me, as did one friend, not the least, that a young man had been raised from the dead at the invocation of Christ, reporting wondrous and dreadful things among the lower regions, narrating the torments of wicked Christians, namely of those who by acting perversely crucified Christ; that they were especially guilty of this, that, forgetful of the benefit of most gracious redemption, they always showed themselves ungrateful to Christ; and that those suffer dreadful things who, known to be ungrateful for his benefits by not living well, and blinded by sin, neglected future joys while following the pleasures of the world. They, bitten by the negligence they had committed, cried out most bitterly: Deservedly we endure these things, we who were always ungrateful to the redeemer of the human race: Christians in name, heathens in deed. We wretches always sought earthly consolations; therefore we receive the due recompense of eternal damnation. Alas, most unhappy that we are: why did we offend Christ? Why did we despise the time granted to us? The raised young man reported to us many deep things, which I am utterly unable to write, especially being weighed down by serious business. And therefore, brother, let us zealously imitate the footsteps of Christ, always giving thanks to our most gentle Savior and asking that he forgive us the guilt we have committed. Farewell. 6 Kalends of April.

When the person to whom the letters are sent, being skilled in the art, has received them, let him observe the lord of the ascendant of the same hour, the sign of the twelfth house; and let him write their characters, with the rest, on paper, together with the other things required for the operation; and afterwards let him say the above-mentioned conjuration, and, when the spirit has been seen, these words: Camerusin apoy-

is sufficient for every operation of the present hour. Conjuration.

Sasquiel adres rhotrofei rosiel emeltto satu olmeniel irsoth sauear nauediel liernoti chameson. When these things have been completed, and the other necessary things added, say the conjuration itself, as is proper; and at once you will see the spirit whom you have called visibly present, to whom you can safely entrust the secret.

Method of announcing the secret.

Let there be for us any sort of secret for a friend, which we wish no one except him to know; and let it be such that it may not safely be entrusted either to letters or to messengers. Let us call one of the companions of the aforesaid Sasquiel; let us entrust the secret to him; let us attach letters sealed with his character, and we shall be safe.

Text of the letter at one’s pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to the religious brother Nicolaus Basellius of Dürkheim, monk of Hirsau, greetings.

You neglect holy obedience, good brother, and humility; you weaken the constitutions of Benedict. Through the report of all who successively come together, he has learned that you hate good zeal, despise the norm of religion and Catholic obedience, and are occupied with secular works and arts. Good brother, what are you doing? You disturb us and foolishly court double-tongued men; you love hatred, bitterness, quarrels, and contentions; you hate goodness; you are double-tongued, contentious, proud. Is it enough

Book Two.

Fool, what are you doing? The time is at hand for correcting these negligent acts of yours more swiftly, zealously, according to justice; and unless you hasten humbly to us to break the zeal of bitterness by the scourges of humiliations, we are compelled by office to be zealous against all the things you are doing that are seditious against the faith and Catholic morals. Farewell from Spanheim, the day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1500.

When he to whom the letters are sent has received them, being skilled in the art, once the character of Sasquiel has been recognized, and the things customarily to be sent ahead have first been sent ahead, let him pronounce the aforesaid conjuration over it; and immediately the spirit sent will appear and present himself visibly. When he has been seen, let him at once say these words: Fabelmerusyn aueual vear cralti penafon. When the said spirit has heard these, he will immediately approach and reveal the secret.

Chapter VI.

Whose Hour Is Called Genapherym.

Its supreme emperor spirit is called Saniel, who has under him 100 dukes, with many servants.

The sixth hour of the day is called Genapherym, and its angel is Saniel, great and powerful in his operations; he has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts, and 5,550 servants assigned to the service of various operations. These suffice for us for everything that we may wish to perform through Steganography in this hour.

The dukes, however, are more rarely summoned, although they are ready and very willing to obey our commands, because their counts are accustomed for the most part to carry out their duties, since they are often occupied in other magical experiments.

Then, after adding what according to the custom of the art must be added, say this conjuration with strong intention, as is fitting, and at once the spirits summoned will appear visibly. Entrust the secret not to the count but to the duke, unless perhaps you have summoned a count without a duke; and although I do not deny that this can be done, nevertheless according to the precept of the art at least one duke must be summoned, with as many counts as you wish.

The subject of the secret, as you wish.

Let the secret be for you whatever sort of matter to a friend that you do not wish to be shared with anyone else. Therefore one should trust neither letters nor notaries, because fraud can intervene everywhere. Summon from the above-named spirits as many as you wish; entrust the secret to the more powerful one, fearing nothing, because they are good and faithful for all things.

The form of the letter is as one pleases.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to the brave soldier Heinrich von Bunau, his most devoted fellow philosopher.

I had lent you my books on condition that they be returned, my very dear soldier Bunau; but behold, you have by no means returned those which you ought shortly to have sent back

Book Two.

...you ought to have. You act against the law which the Catholic faith has established concerning a promise: do not delay to pay to all what you promised. It is not fitting for a good and honorable man, born of noble parents and ancestors, to violate a promise. You had promised, however, to restore them very soon and with the greatest diligence. It is fickleness to put off a promise, as it were, to the Greek Kalends. Have I not waited long enough with great goodwill? To promise very great things is most shameful for one who returns the least. Good faith adorns a soldier. What more serious crime than to refuse a loaned thing promised for return? Nor is it fitting for a Christian to be unwilling to keep an agreement. The ordinance of Christian law commands one to keep a promise, to return a loan; what you desire to be done to you, you should gladly do also to others. I demand back my books, which I had lent to you at your entreaty. Put aside the longer excuses, which you promise for the Greek Kalends. You know my mind in brief. Consider your name and the honorable family of the Bunawenses, and send my volumes back to me. Farewell. From Spanheim, 2 April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When you have received these letters, or any others whatsoever, from him who sent the spirit to you, after recognizing the sign of Barquiel, observe in that same hour the lord of the ascendant; write his character, together with the others, on a clean sheet. You will read secretly the written conjuration on the back, as is proper; at once the spirit that was sent will appear. As soon as you have seen him, say these words to him: Mefarym burne theoralueas casuean cralti lierto aply charmoys.

When these have been said, the sent spirit, coming nearer, will faithfully reveal to you the secret committed to him. But see that you are strong, steadfast, and undaunted in all things.

Chapter VIII.

Whose hour is called Iafanym, and whose angel is called Osmadiel; he has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts. The number of servants is uncertain.

The eighth hour of the day is called Iafanym; its principal spirit is named Osmadiel, according to Picatrix in the magical writings. He has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts, and innumerable servants, assigned not only to the operation of our Steganography, but also to many magical experiments. And Solomon the Jew, surnamed Hermes, says in the book On the Nature of Spirits that all those dukes and counts obedient and subject to the aforesaid Osmadiel are accustomed to come in various transformations according to the will of the operator, just as they have been commanded by the operator. But now let us set down the names of some of them.

Sarfiel, Demaros, Mariel: 10, 10, 100, 100. Amalym, Ianofiel, Remasyn: 10, 10, 100, 100. Chroel, Larfuty, Theoriel: 10, 10, 100, 100. Mesial, Vemael, Framion: 10, 10, 100, 100. Lantribotz, Thribiel, Ermiel: 10, 10, 100, 100.

Of the dukes five, and of the counts ten, we now have named in the table; they suffice for us for every operation of this hour. When, however, you wish to work through them in Steganography, write on a clean slip with the customary characters and conjurations; and, first adding the following things to those that must be added, speak the written conjuration itself, which is as follows.

Conjuration.

O Smodael aneor ersotynes as, hays layr Caphrayn thelreas meair penarsy.

When this song of conjuration has been spoken, the spirits called will be present, ready and obedient for all things. Entrust the secret to the duke, not to the count, unless the former is absent, because it must always be entrusted to the more principal one among those who come.

An Example of a Secret at Will.

Let there be for us any secret whatever, which we wish a far-distant friend to know, and such that we do not wish it to come to anyone’s

Book Two.

the knowledge of another; and it can often happen. Therefore, lest either the courier reveal the secret on some occasion, or the letters come into foreign hands, let us act; through the spirit we shall be safe.

John Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, sends greeting to Lord Conrad, Abbot of Saint Stephen at Wurzburg.

A report has gone out concerning the Abbot of Limburg, that he has dismissed Brother John of Feilsdorf, a faithful man, highly skilled in temporal affairs, and has introduced new [unclear] monks, and appointed them as his officials. I greatly marvel at the useless deed. Nevertheless, when I remember the custom of the Limburgers, I do not know what to say. For they are ignorant of temporal matters, and therefore they dismissed a faithful man, because he reproved their deeds; they ought to have given thanks to our Savior Jesus Christ for the fidelity of so great a brother, who could have revealed their necessities. Wretched men, why do you reject a good and necessary helper? What shall I say? I do not praise the departure of so useful a brother. They have appointed stewards over temporal affairs. Abbot Muchar, it did not befit a man to act thus. At first you praised him; now you have rejected a man very necessary to you, and to be placed after none. I confess that if Christ had given him to me, as befits a Christian I would now give the greatest thanks, and would take care that he never departed. But you, ungrateful to Christ, preferred, by the foolish counsel of wicked men, to dismiss a faithful man who had been wearied, lest, with your affairs abandoned, there should seem to be any hope of recovery. From Sponheim, 3 Nones of April, 1500.

When the person to whom these letters, or any others whatsoever, have been sent has received them, sealed with the sign of Osmadael, being skilled in the art, after the preliminaries have been performed, let him say the prescribed conjuration; immediately the spirit sent will appear visibly. Of these, for the service of this art of ours of Steganography, 10 of the dukes and 100 of the counts have been assigned; they have many servants assigned to themselves in orders. In the first order there are 10, in the second 20, in the third 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 500, in the sixth 600, in the seventh 700, in the eighth 1,080, in the ninth 90,000, but in the tenth there are 100,000. Raziel the Great, however, said in his book on illusions and transformations that the number of these spirits is very great, and that each one most diligently keeps his own orders in all services; and Solomon Hermes the Jew says, concerning the nature of spirits, that these are accustomed to appear in that form which the one working in the art has described, according to his will. The Theme of the Secret.

A secret of whatever kind comes to us for a friend, which we wish to be most secret and in no way revealed to anyone except him. Therefore let us call one or two from the aforesaid dukes and counts, according to the instruction of the art, and let us entrust the secret to the more powerful one.

Let us form letters at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to the religious father Johannes Hugo, guardian of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis in Kreuznach, greeting and charity.

Reverend and venerable father in religion, I know that you gladly grant suitable things to all friends; therefore I humbly beseech you, that in view of Catholic piety you not take it ill that your [unclear] brothers, detained rather long with us with the greatest charity, [unclear]; for it was necessary that they remain, at my entreaty. It was a glorious joy for us, while we all rejoiced without offense. We exulted in the Lord with spiritual joy, giving thanks to almighty God with good zeal. What gathering, I ask, is more religious than such a one? where nothing idle is said, nothing unjust is pursued with zeal; may Christ Jesus, the savior of all, make us rejoice in everlasting glory.

Glorious zealots of the virtues place nothing before truth. Filled with holy joy, we pray that you receive the aforesaid brothers peacefully and lay aside every zeal of bitterness. Farewell from Sponheim, 3 Nones of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When you, being skilled in the art, have received these letters or any others marked with the character of Quabriel, after the things to be sent ahead have first been sent ahead, say the prescribed conjuration. The tenth hour of the day is called Lamarhon, and its supreme angel is called Oriel, a great and powerful emperor, who, according to Solomon the Jew, has under his rule many dukes and counts who, together with their attendants, are assigned to the operation of Steganography. In the first order there are 10, in the sixth 30, in the fourth 40, in the fifth 500, in the sixth 600, in the seventh 700, in the eighth 800, in the ninth 900, in the tenth 1000. But we, taking only 10 counts from the first five orders and only five dukes from the last, are content in our operations. If it pleases anyone to know the names of more, let him call one of those named in the table and question him; and he will hear whatever he wishes, and however many he wishes to know, he will know them perfectly from him.

Formulation of the Secret.

We have a friend whose welfare we favor; we fear that he is to be supplanted and circumvented by some wandering rogue. Therefore we desire that he be warned. We cannot do it in plain words by messengers; by letters, lest they fall into someone’s hands, likewise we dare not. Therefore, so that we may be safe and our secret may always remain hidden, let us call at least one spirit, the leader of those named above. He comes, obeys, and faithfully carries the message.

Let the letter be composed at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Heinrich von Bünau, golden knight, distinguished philosopher and mathematician.

Since you are a most devoted student of the humanities, you will rejoice, I think, exceedingly to have found a new companion in your studies. The man who will present this letter to you is a man of great knowledge, a supreme philosopher, a most subtle arithmetician, a most eloquent rhetorician, a very profound mathematician, and in every respect most excellently learned. He speaks with the greatest elegance, resplendent with Ciceronian eloquence. For if I were most especially your friend, I would have kept so great a man wholly to myself, since in using his services I have found him a most learned philosopher. I especially favor you; receive gladly the philosopher whom, moved by singular affection, I send to you. O would that all our students were such, who with timid heart scorn noble knowledge. This man constantly searches into the study of philosophy and the lofty sciences, and the most lofty and profound things of nature; he continually handles them and penetrates them most acutely. Therefore, Heinrich Bünau, remember for Christ’s sake to treat the man with a generous countenance. Farewell from Sponheim, 2 November, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When the friend to whom the letter is sent, skilled in this science of Steganography, has received the letter, let him do everything that according to the art must be done, and let him append the conjuration written above, as is customary. The tenor of the letters at pleasure.

Ioannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Brother Quirinus, a monk of Corbie in France, greeting.

Concerning the mother of the perpetual Virgin Mary, I send my prayer, which you recently requested, Quirinus: Hail, most gracious mother Anna, most radiant parent of the Virgin Mary; you most faithful helper of all who call upon you; you noble refuge of those who seek you; quiet benefit of holiness. Hail, most gentle advocate of the poor; most beautiful consoler of those who groan; most adorned storehouse of virtues. Hail, [Iuda?], restorer of the sorrowful; most healthful medicine of the sick; and most celebrated promoter of faithful Christians. Obtain pardon for us as we pray; soften Christ, the dread judge; intercede for your servants, that we may attain blessedness; with you interceding, we ask that in his kindness he receive us miserable ones. Amen. The eighth day before the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

The theme of any secret whatever, at pleasure, that occurs.

We have a friend absent far away. We know that a danger threatens him, of which he is unaware. We desire to warn him, but for certain reasons we do not dare to do so openly. Therefore we call the spirits assigned to this operation according to the hour, and safely commend the secret.

Letters, formed at pleasure, we seal with the sign of the spirit.

Everyone who glories in temporal things is by no means left to be called virtuous; and he who loves transitory things cannot be a lover of justice, since Catholic integrity detests a man gaping after desires. For the holy religion of the Christian faith forbids love of the world to its people, since he who loves worldly joys loses heavenly happiness. A Catholic who does not live as a Catholic is shown to have denied Christ; and he who loves temporal things is not called a good Catholic. He who loves the Creator seeks the joys of spiritual things. The lover of Christ [unclear] all the pleasures of the world

Book Two.

...despises pleasures and does not care for glory and unstable riches. But the lover of the world hates the virtues; he cares nothing for future joys. Alas, what are you doing, Christians, intent on vain things? You are thinking things that are not honorable and will do things contrary to religion. Do not, I beseech you, do not love the soon-to-perish vanities of this world. Take care rather to love Christ, so that he may receive us into the heavenly kingdoms. Ioan. Tritt. Abb.

A secret is made, whatever occurs to us, great and arduous.

The secret which we wish to communicate to a friend through spirits is made whatever may occur to us at the time and according to the variety of affairs, so that it is not trivial, nor of such a kind that it can otherwise be safely reported.

Johannes Trithemius, to the nuns on Mount Saint Rupert, who adorn the Catholic faith with bright virginity, continuously to merit eternal happiness by the most holy zeal of religion.

By the mercy of the eternal King, we providently send you, after he has been long awaited, a man of great experience in temporal affairs, Johannes, born of Raunenstat, for a long time reverend and zealous abbot of the monastery of Violsdorf, and freely resigning that same abbey. On his account, as I had promised you, I went to the monastery of Lunapurga, in which he was serving Christ, occupied with continual prayers and readings of the holy Scriptures, with the monks of that same monastery; and I asked that he come down to your convent and undertake the care of temporal affairs, and become procurator and cellarer. The abbot of Lympurg, with his usual instability, changed in mind, [unclear] I was able to obtain his consent to dismiss him. At last, by Christ’s inspiration, he consented, though fearfully, because he fears to serve nuns, who change very readily. He is not without reason afraid, since, as experience has taught us, nuns have sometimes repaid their stewards for benefits with a reward not praiseworthy. A feminine spirit suddenly [changes] into zeal of bitterness. Yet, with Christ granting it, I know that he will be useful to you. He is a Christian, he is a monk, he fears the Savior, and he is of good understanding. Therefore accustom yourselves to restrain feminine mutability, so that you may remember to be constant; receiving him with holy honor and sincere charity, laying aside every levity of feminine spirit, especially since, with the help of Christ the Redeemer, who is zealous for charity, he can assist you and restore the condition of temporal affairs collapsed in your monastery. Farewell. From Sponheim, 17 Kalends of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

To the venerable father in Christ, steward of the Lympurgenses, the religious lord called Johannes Weißdorffen, John Ouilis, humble abbot of Spanheim, joy of the heavens.

The nuns of Saint Rupert desire you with exceeding eagerness as their governor, and humbly ask you in goodwill to undertake the governance of the temporal affairs of that monastery. To serve the devout virgins of Christ is praiseworthy and meritorious. You have, in spiritual affairs of the same convent, an excellent and most renowned visitor, who embraces you with the greatest honor: grave in conduct, adorned with virtues, cautious in counsel, beloved by all, well reputed in the life of monastic religion, and notable to all men; and such a life is deservedly most pleasing to Christ: the excellent abbot of the monastery of Saint John. He is most learned, most studious, and most skilled in the writings both of Christians and of pagans, and he notably far surpasses the wisdom of all men. He knows very well how to govern the flock entrusted to him, and he is a very zealous guardian of the virgins of Christ, whose cloister he preserves most firmly. Do not fear to serve such honorable nuns under him, who knows how to govern the brides of Christ according to the monastic law with the best discretion. By the virtue and zeal of the Christian faith he will gladly come to your aid in necessity. Since you have this man, so famous and kindly, as an intimate friend, I profess that you should gladly assume the helm of so religious virgins. Christ will reward your labor with eternal joys. May the Bridegroom, protector, and most kindly rewarder of the nuns grant you, with good zeal, to strive after better things. Farewell. From Spanheim, 15 Kalends of May, in the year 1500.

The Catholic faith saves no one who despises the ardor of divine love. To believe and not to have zeal for divine love is of no use at all for the redemption of the soul. Moreover, many people are now found who boast of the Catholic faith, but few have the works of the Christian faith; but idle faith dies. Many believe, but very few observe the commandments of God. Alas, the zeal of believers is weak; even unbelieving people can have a stronger zeal than this, and many do have it. Gentiles and people who do not believe that our savior, made man, is the son of the Almighty will be tormented by the punishments of hell. But all those who believe that the Son of God came into the world and became man through zeal for human redemption, yet do not adorn the Christian faith with holy works, and, always entangled in sins, prefer the honors of the world to eternal blessedness, zealously pursuing impious actions and staining the purity of faith with corrupt morals against obedience, will be tortured with heavier punishments. But the lovers of God, who have the right zeal of the Christian faith, prefer nothing to God, imitate Christ, flee sins, and despise the riches and honors of the world. Now therefore attend to these words, you who glory in faith: love God, and you will have the reward of blessedness, pursuing righteousness. If you love the vanities of the age against the honor of God, you will receive the prize of those who pursue iniquity: the horrors of hell. Written on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Adam of Fulda, solitary doctor of the arts and of philosophy, greeting and charity.

Remember your promise, which, when receiving the Catholic faith, you offered to Christ with a solemn vow. Eternal joy, which has been promised to all by [unclear] or sordid things? Without doubt it is promised to those who, in view of the eternal rest to come, despise the temporal pleasures and joys of the present life, and who love the eternal God. We know that the best rewards have been promised to the lovers of God; but for the lovers of the world and reprobate Christians God has prepared the most bitter punishments of hell. He who has faith, but neglects to have divine love, is an unbeliever and also presumes vainly about faith. A zealot of divine love, who does not cease daily to adorn the Christian faith with devout and good works, exercising himself humbly in the arts of piety. Farewell. 18 April, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1500.

Let us form letters at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, sends greeting to Nicolaus Basselius, monk, and transmits this prayer of Saint Nicholas.

Creator of all things, reformer and maker, created the first man, Adam, to whom he joined a very beautiful wife named Eve, the mother of all living things, prefiguring the Catholic Church, to be joined to shepherds, shining beautifully with the morals of uprightness, and destined to bear sons of good works, men who by humility obtain the kingdoms of heaven that will remain without end. Christ redeemed us through his most kindly love for us; he gave us the Catholic faith, and those who truly love it will rightly obtain angelic happiness. Therefore let us all, living in true religion and living as Catholics, daily honor our almighty creator. Lord Jesus, most kindly savior, who mercifully redeemed us all from the abyss of death, kindly regarding our frailty and weakness, conform us to the Catholic faith, so that after this transitory life we may deserve to have forever the rest of eternal consolation and happiness. Amen. 14 Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Let us form letters at will.

O most gracious Jesus, I give thanks to your most holy mercy: you who by your blood reconciled the human race to the heavenly Father, hanging piteously raised upon the Cross; you subjected for our sake the flourishing youth of your most noble body to harsh wounds, so that you might make dead man live. Therefore, let us Catholics give such thanks as we can to our redeemer: groaning and praising, recalling in Christian fashion the memory of the passion of the savior of our race. Have mercy on me, most merciful Jesus, fount of mercy, abyss of compassion, glory of the saints, light of the citizens above; and pour into me the sweetest taste of your most holy love. Deliver me from all my calamities. Give me true gladness of heart, that I may exult in your praises, glorifying you, since by the pain of your wounds you have healed me. What shall I render to your mercy, my Redeemer, my giver of life? I have compassion for your sufferings with burning tears, and, blessing the most holy wounds of your body, most gracious Savior Jesus, I give thanks, asking pardon for my crimes. In the year of the Lord 1500, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, I wrote this prayer, τυμβοὶ λαοῦ τε γῆ μου.

Wail, mortals, you who now laugh: by your very grave sins and horrible crimes you have in many ways most ungratefully spurned the kindness also of our glorious redeemer. Behold, the Turk, the deadly enemy of Christians, will move his army from Hungary; he will slaughter men like beasts. Savage, kindled with zeal for impiety as if with fire, he has crossed the Danube. Therefore mourn, most wretched ones, doomed to die in horrible slaughter; you will die in bitter zeal, because your crimes will seize you. You have despised the laws of God, your most gracious redeemer. Therefore you will be handed over to most cruel enemies, who will devour you like locusts. We have heard how cruelly the Turk invaded Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland; he destroyed very strong cities; women and virgins consecrated to God, holding chastity in zeal for holiness, he most shamefully violated, horribly slaughtering all Catholic men, raging everywhere like cruel beasts. This is the prophecy of Nicolaus Basselius of Hirsau, bishop and saint, which he saw in Spicatus. And he said: Thus says the Lord to the shepherds of the churches. Soon you will perish, because a very great calamity will scatter your broad dominion and will sprinkle all Europe. Woe to the Ishmaelites, who break the covenants of the tabernacle, because through envy and rashness they seize Easter. Behold, the dominion that you have will be broken unless you hasten greater repentance; and you will be handed over to be torn apart. Alas, the whole Church has been overturned by the worst morals; pretense has invaded its ministers. Flee; do not look back. You will be laid waste, and you will be dragged by dogs; they will sprinkle the whole land with blood. Therefore, inhabitants of the earth, do penance. Young Benjamin will experience disturbances. Woe to the inhabitants of Gennesaret, which is Europe, because on account of the multitude of their sins they will perish under the hands of the Bulgarians. Here ends the prophecy of Nicolaus, bishop of Hirsau, 12 Kalends of May.

154 Of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim. To Cornelius Gyrardus of Gouda, canon of St. Augustine near Leiden, greetings. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the most gentle savior of our souls, promised us the happiness of eternal consolation, if [unclear] his commandments with a pure [unclear]. Dearest brother, keep diligently the commandments of God and of the holy rule, because unless you preserve inviolate until death all the things that almighty God has commanded you, you will perish by eternal death. Therefore I have handed on to you the form and law of a religious and holy way of life.

Beware, then, diligently, lest you give your heart to be possessed by any mortal creature through the desire of love, because no one comes to those highest joys except the one who despises the world for God. Again, therefore, through this letter of mine I exhort you, as my dearest friend, to observe the warnings that I had given you. For I think that I am doing something good when I write something good in this sacred time, especially for edification concerning the manner of living well, by which you may always become better. Therefore now again I write to you for your good, because I fear your danger no less than my own. But I beg you: always keep watch, advancing daily in the fear of God, and living innocent, harming no one, and altogether persevering in your holy purpose. Do not trust in time, nor fortune, nor age, because they are nothing but smoke. Truly I love you sincerely in Christ Jesus, praying that he himself may arrange that I also be beloved to you; and that I, who am absent from you in body, may always be present in spirit. Therefore, since I continually keep remembrance of you in my prayers, I very earnestly beg you not to forget me. Farewell. 12 Kalends of May, in the year 1500.

Chapter XXIV.

Whose hour is called Xephan, and its angel, called the supreme emperor, is Sarandiel, having under him many princes, dukes, counts, and servants.

The twelfth hour of the night, which reaches the dawn, is called Xephan, and its angel is called Sarandiel, who has under his command many spirits, good and evil, princes, dukes, counts, and ministers, who are assigned to various operations: the good to good ones, and the evil to evil ones. These princes, as Hermes the Hebrew, who is called Solomon, says in the fourth book on the offices of spirits, are accustomed often to appear in that form in which the Devil is read to have appeared to Eve, having one beautiful head like that of a maiden, with hair hanging down on either side, but two serpent-bodies, which nevertheless they always veil and hide under certain coverings or leaves, so that they may not be seen. In face, however, they are most beautiful, benevolent, and pleasant, and most ready and cheerful for every obedience to the operator.

O wretched man, and truly pitiable, why do you not attend to the instability of all temporal things? And why do you not consider that you will shortly die? Remember what the first man deserved because he violated the commandment. Would that, as Balaam wished, our soul might die the death of the righteous, so that, scorning present pleasures and the vain honors of the world, we may be unstained, keeping ourselves from every sin. But we do not take care, until at last we fall into the dreadful bonds of death, to be tormented forever. I consider happy the man who thinks of these things beforehand. Therefore, O man, cast away the world, as the Son of God did, and consider how many evils follow us from love of it. For many dangers are brought upon us, and because it is damnable to those who love it, it is rightly despised. Worthy of eternal death is the lover of the world. What does that world profit you, wretched man? When it is loved, it flees; while it is present, it passes away; while it exalts, it [unclear]; while it flatters, it deceives; while it flourishes, it withers; when it sends forth its lovers, it hands them over to perpetual miseries. Chapter 25.

In which we shall teach the general method and form of approaching this art of Steganography, and of operating in it without danger, with the greatest usefulness.

Whoever desires to approach the knowledge of this hidden art of ours; whoever wishes to work wonders through it, and things useful to many amid dangers: first of all he must be adorned with virtues, and be of clean conscience and good will toward God, toward himself, and toward his neighbor, so that he is not inclined to harm anyone, nor seeks dealings of baseness. Then it is necessary that he be somewhat imbued with the good arts of letters, and especially with the science of the stars, so that he may know the general motions, courses, wanderings, changes, orders, natures, positions, risings, settings, and effects of the stars, signs, and planets; because without competent knowledge of these no one can have access to the depths of this art. Consequently it is necessary that he have a teacher perfect and experienced in the art, because we believe it possible to come to this science without a teacher only for a few, and for those most learned in many things, and especially skilled in magical matters. But the teacher must be not only proven and experienced in knowledge, but also faithful, upright, and fearing God; because the purer he has been in good conduct with God, the safer he will be in the operation of this science. For the spirits obey virtues. Therefore, when anyone is about to approach this art, let the teacher receive him and lead him into some secret and clean place. Let the time be tranquil and clear, and

Of the Steganography ... and the moon in complete opposition, with the sun shining clearly; and let Mercury be in the ascendant, joined to Venus or Jupiter, if possible; and let Saturn and Mars be remote, because if they themselves, or either of them, are with the ascendant, the initiation will not be perfect. First of all the person to be initiated in the art shall swear an oath: I, N., swear and promise by the power of almighty God, by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the resurrection of the dead and the last judgment, and by the salvation of my soul in the holy Catholic faith, to almighty God, to the blessed Virgin Mary, to all the saints, and to you, N., that I will faithfully keep this art of Steganography hidden all the days of my life, nor will I teach it to anyone without your will and consent. Moreover, by the same power I swear and promise that I will not use this science against God and his commandments, nor against the holy Roman and universal Church or its ministers, nor against justice and equity. So may God help me, and so may he save me at the last judgment. Then the preceptor shall read the following conjuration in the mystical tongue, and shall interpret it, and all the conjurations contained in this work, before the disciple, lest he suspect that there is anything diabolical, superstitious, or contrary to God, or that any compact with demons, implicit or explicit, is in any way secretly hidden there.

Here begins the third book of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, addressed to the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Empire.

Preface.

After, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of faithful souls, we had completed the first two books of our art, in which we described our Steganography as best we could, we must join this third book to them, and link more marvelous things to marvelous discoveries. I found in a certain book of a certain ancient philosopher, who was called Menaistor, that it is possible, by a certain art, for us to make known the conception of our mind to a friend, however absent he may be, without hours, without words, without books, and without a messenger, most perfectly, most broadly, and most secretly. And since I was driven very vehemently by a desire to know, I began to wish to test the truth of the statements; and after many labors at last I found that very science proven by experience. Very great is

Preface.

The secret of this art is of such a kind, and wrapped in such great obscurities, that it is not easily accessible to anyone. For Menastor enveloped the mystery very obscurely and in few words, and he used such powers to keep it secret that after him no one has yet been found who has dared to make his discourse clearer by any instruction. But I, fearing that so marvelous a work, because of its excessive obscurity, might be despised by the unskilled, or at last burned in the fire, since I have long since tested it by many proofs, wished to commit it to writing in clearer letters, so that, with God's help, it might in some measure become accessible to learned men and to those most devoted to magical studies; and yet it should at all times remain hidden from unskilled Rapophagi, and in no way become known to their dull understanding.

But Menastor said: There are seven planets, over which seven angels preside, and under them are subject twenty-one spirits, through whom secrets are announced. Let us set out their names by means of a table.
