Preface.

These are the seven angels, according to the tradition of the ancient sages, each of whom guides the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months in his order. Orifiel is the angel of Saturn, who from the beginning of creation governed the world for 354 years and 4 months. Afterwards Venus, then Jupiter, after him Mercury, and then Mars, afterwards the Moon, afterwards the Sun. Each is described as having held dominion over the world for 354 years and 4 months, with his angel written in the table common to him. And so the sages report that at the time of the flood Samael, the angel of Mars, served the authority of rule; Gabriel, however, the angel of the Moon, at the time of the confusion of tongues; Michael, the angel of the Sun, at the time of Israel's departure from Egypt. And indeed, if anyone gives credence to the aforesaid assertion, he will easily be able by himself, from the origin of the world down to his own age, to calculate the changes of times and the governance of the angels in the order prescribed. But we, pursuing those things that serve our purpose, do not doubt that under the seven aforesaid angels of the planets there are subject twenty-one other spirits, that is, three to each one, according to the instruction of this art of ours; through them we accomplish the effect of our intention. We shall observe the customary order of the planets, beginning from Saturn, the highest of all, down to the Moon, first writing down the operation of each principal angel, and then of those serving under them, and joining the chapters together in order.

Chapter I

On Orifiel, the first and supreme angel of Saturn, and on the operations that are performed through him.

Saturn, the highest and supreme of all the planets, slow in motion and by nature, cold because remote, difficult, heavy, from the point of its beginning 650 years up to the point of its first station, remaining in each sign for 30 months, is moved by its natural proper motion 626. Its first and supreme angel is called, according to the opinion of the ancients, Orifiel, who has under him three other principal spirits, namely Sadael, Poniel, and Morisiel, of whom we shall speak in their proper place and order.

Through this Orifiel, the great angel of Saturn, many different operations are performed in steganography. Through him we can make the secret of our mind known to a friend who knows the art, wherever he may be: by letters, if one wishes, or even without letters, and do many other marvelous things, which no one else understands who is unskilled in this science of ours. Therefore, anyone wishing to perform anything through this angel in steganography, especially on the day of Saturn, in these matters, business, and causes that pertain to Saturn, must first know its various and diverse motions. And first the various motion: pure, proper, mixed, direct, retrograde, and confused. And in all these he must know not only the general rules handed down by the astronomers, because although they are very useful for this science of ours, nevertheless they do not wholly suffice, but also the particular rules.

Therefore, once the tables and rules concerning the motions of the planets have been laid down as a foundation, which anyone working in this art must know completely, we have added special rules and tables of punctual motions throughout the individual chapters of this work; without observing them no one will be able to operate in this art. And note that the day of each planet is divided into four equal parts, of which the principal angel of that planet obtains the first, that is, three unequal hours; and his substitutes in order take the remaining three parts. For example: on the day of Saturn, Orifiel, its first angel, possesses the three unequal hours from sunrise, which are called the hours of the planets; Sadael, his first angel, possesses the second three; Pomiel, the second, holds the third; and Morisiel, the third angel of Orifiel, holds the last three hours. In the first three hours of the day both of Saturn and of the other stars, in matters appropriated to Saturn, one must operate through Orifiel; in the second, through Sadael; in the third, through Pomiel; and in the last three, through Morisiel. And all operations, according to the motion of Saturn, receive either a prosperous effect or a weak one. But now let us set down the punctual table.

Punctual table.

[table of numbers and unclear characters] The order of the letters written in black [unclear].

Of Steganography.

When the mean motion of Saturn for the second day, degree, and hour has been learned from the common tables, know that it must first be carefully observed whether it is direct or retrograde; pure, proper, mixed, or confused. But you will not find this from the common tables. For that reason we have arranged the prescribed table, in which you will be able to find the point of the beginning and [end?] of its motion at any hour, the degrees being divided, with intervening [unclear], into particles of minutes. That is, each minute is to be divided into two, three, or four hourly parts, according to the proportion of the pure or confused motion, that is, with the conjunction or separation of the other planets observed. For it is impossible, either through the stars or through the spirits of the stars, for you to arrive at the effect of this art unless, with the knowledge of the punctual motion most diligently observed, you know how to order your operations precisely according to the proper qualities of the planets. For in different degrees, signs, days, hours, minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths, the effects of the planets, with respect to this science, vary in different ways. For in each degree we have observed and found twenty-five different changes; hence it seemed necessary to us to divide each degree into just as many principal parts. This division, however, does not apply throughout all the degrees, but only in those in which the stars conducive to this art rise for us, with which the operation is performed for signifying to the absent everything that we wish, by the ministry of spirits, without letters, as we shall say. Therefore the first table of the division of the degrees of the motion of Saturn, which we have set forth above, serves perpetually for the first quarter of the day or night in those things which pertain to the operation of Saturn and its beginnings; the second, however, for the second three hours; the third for the third; the fourth for the fourth. Then we have added the punctual order of the motion of Saturn itself in the ascendant, namely when it shall have been in one of the first four signs, which are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer. We shall also arrange a following table concerning the remaining eight signs.

R. † 2 Concerning at the degree of Aries, point 641, [unclear] and 69, we have included the whole Zodiac in the second table. Then, in the same second table, we have arranged the motion of Saturn in any one of the twelve signs, for all the quarters of the day and night, down to the minutes, so that, at whatever hour, once the degree of the ascendant in which Saturn himself is has been known by us, the precise root of it may be able to appear clearly. But once the calculation of something has been completed, to which I do not know whether our age can ever attain, the table must be begun anew from the head of its beginning. In the third table we have reduced to proportion the sevenfold conjunction of Saturn with the other planets, which is unique; through it all 120 conjunctions are easily reduced to the point. In the same table the pure motion of all the planets is known through the punctual division of each beginning, progression, and elongation from the point in any motion, if the mean motion has first been perfectly obtained. For without knowledge of the mean motion it is impossible for anyone to be able to approach the practice of this science. Again, even if you understand the mean motion and likewise the true motion most perfectly, it will profit you nothing for knowledge of this science unless you understand fully the three prescribed tables for all the points of the divisions in the motions of the planets, taken equally from unequal degrees, minute by minute. But now let us proceed to the operation.

When, however, all these things have been known, and those things which we have said, and, with God’s help, are going to say, have been perfectly understood, when you wish to work in this most profound speculation, first of all you must know the rising, elevation, and setting of all the stars of the eighth sphere, through which the operation is made, and how far each is distant from another. The stars through which we operate for announcing any secret whatever to an absent person, whether by words or by writings and without a human messenger, are seven hundred in number. Their names, places, risings, settings, elevations, distances, approaches, and recessions we have described in a special book; it would be too laborious to repeat them here again by inserting them. Therefore, when the star has been observed in all respects as is proper, and when the point of the ascendant in which Saturn was at that same hour has been known, if the operation is made through him, consider most diligently the quality of its motion

LIBERTIUS.

[unclear] before you on the table or lectern. And concerning the conjuration appropriated to the Spirit through whom you work. Or, if you prefer to announce the secret entirely without writings, through the Spirit or without the Spirit, this is placed at your discretion. For it is an operation of the same kind to announce a secret to a friend with the Spirit or without the Spirit, a few things being altered, as we shall say in its place. Now we shall set out the difference of the operations of Saturn and of his Angels according to the four principal quarters, with the conjurations appropriated to each in order; these are to be used when you announce a secret through the Spirit.

On the first Angel of Saturn, who is principal, and is called Orifiel, who observes the first quarter of Saturn.

[unclear]

The first and principal angel of Saturn, as we have said in the preceding sections, is called Orifiel; he, with the other angels of the planets in his order, rules the sphere for 354 years and four months. He has the first part both in the day and in the night; and through him the operation is performed from sunrise in the day, and from sunset in the night, up to the third hour inclusive, in all things that pertain to Saturn, and on his day and night, as we have said. Therefore, when in the first quarter of Saturn you wish to announce something to one absent without words and without letters, then no Spirit of Saturn other than Orifiel is to be summoned by you, because through him you will be able to announce everything most perfectly. First consider in what sign this Saturn is, and in what degree, and whether he is direct or retrograde, and with what planets he is in conjunction. Let us set down an example of the first point: Behold, Saturn is now in the 25th degree of Taurus, on the 28th day of the month of April in the present year, which is the year of the Lord 1500. Now therefore let us multiply 25, and they become 600; let us divide these by the four equal quarters, and there will remain to each quarter 150. Let us complete all the degrees of Saturn in the sign of Taurus, and there will be 30. But let us multiply 3 by 25 in all, and they become 750. Let us cast off the four superfluous degrees from the middle of the third quarter, and 650 will remain. Now let us take the point of Saturn’s motion from the table for the present day and hour; and we shall be able to know what is the rising, elevation, and setting of the Angel Orifiel with Saturn in the first quarter. Once these are known, our operation will be easy.

When these things have been most diligently considered, it is clear that Orifiel of Saturn is separated from Saturn by 25 degrees and 15 minutes; he is toward the east, distant from the first point of Saturn’s motion by 625 gradations, and from the end of the motion by 25 minutes. When these things are known, make an image out of wax, or paint on new paper the figure of Orifiel in the likeness of a bearded and naked man, standing upon a bull of varied color, holding in his right hand a book, and in his left a reed-pen. While you are making it, say: Let this image of great Orifiel be full, perfect, and fit to announce the secret of my mind to N., son of N., my friend, securely, faithfully, and completely. Amen. Write on the forehead your own name with ink tempered with oil of roses, and on the breast the name of your absent friend, saying: This is the image of N., son of N., to whom through Orifiel, angel of Saturn, the conception of my mind is announced. Amen. On the forehead of the image write Merion, and on the breast Troesda. Then join both images together, saying: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Hear, Orifiel, prince of the star of Saturn, and by the powers of almighty God I adjure you, listen: I command and order you, by the power of this image of yours, that you announce to N., son of N., this intention of mine (let the intention be explained) as quickly as possible, securely, secretly, and faithfully, omitting nothing of those things which I want him to know, and which I have entrusted to you. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Then wrap those images, thus fastened together, in a cloth washed with water of white [wine?], and put them in a movable vessel, which the wise call Indix pharnat alronda; cover it carefully above with shaved leather, and put it in the entrance of some closed dwelling, wherever you wish, for the space of 24 hours; and without any hesitation your desire will be perfectly fulfilled within those 24 hours. And your absent friend will know your intention in every form most perfectly, just as you spoke it over the image, however long it may have been; and whatever you wish him to know from you, he will know within those 24 hours perfectly and most secretly, so that no man will ever be able to perceive or know this for all eternity without your will or that of your friend. And it is a great secret, which none of the wise before us dared to commit to writing. But that friend of yours, if he wishes you to know anything from his affairs, can make you more certain through the same spirit within the same space of 24 hours, provided he is well perfected in this art. But you, when 24 hours have elapsed, take the images from the place in which they were put, and put them away, because at every time of Orifiel you can operate through them not only for that friend of yours, but for any others whatsoever, merely changing the name of that friend into the name of the person whom you wish to know something. And note that the images themselves need not be painted beautiful or elaborate; however simple they may be, it makes no difference, provided they have some proportionate likeness, so that they are recognized as images of men. But if anyone wishes and is able to paint them beautifully, it will not hinder, nor does it help.

Concerning the second angel of Saturn, who is the first under Orifiel and is called Sadael, presiding over the second quarter of Saturn.

The second angel of Saturn is called Sadael, who is appointed first under Orifiel in order, and has the second part after his prince, both by day and by night, in the works and times of Saturn: that is, the fourth, fifth, and sixth unequal hours. Therefore, when in these three hours you wish to announce something to an absent friend within twenty-four hours, without letters, without words, and without a messenger, do it in all respects and by the sign which we stated in the preceding operation; and observe the point of the second motion of Saturn in its degrees toward the sign in which that planet itself is moved, and what the motion is like, and where the spirit moving the star is, how far it has receded, and how far it is elevated from the center of its motion, however far it is distant from any point of the whole circle or sphere. To attain knowledge of these things, this is the table.

Key to the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

To the Most Serene Prince Lord Philipp, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Elector of the Empire.

For sale at the shop of Johann Berner, bookseller of Frankfurt, in the year 1608. With privilege and the consent of the superiors.

Preface of Johannes Trithemius

It is the opinion of the wise that the ancient philosophers of art and nature, who had discovered secrets, concealed them by various methods and figures, so that they might not come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews also confirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth, disclosed ineffable mysteries of secrets in simple words. Saint Jerome, most learned among our own, says that in the Apocalypse almost as many mysteries lie hidden as there are words. Moreover, the wise men of the Greeks, of no small esteem among their own people, who devoted their effort to writing fables, with most prudent reasoning handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to the wise in the course of a single narration. I cannot but admire these most zealous lovers of wisdom, and I do not fail to read them with whatever industry I can, so that, while I consider that they labored by lamplight more greatly than other men, I may, as best I can, fill the empty belly of my memory with certain crumbs, as it were, of knowledge falling from the table of the rich philosophers.

Nor, as I think, has this opinion altogether deceived me, since by the continual labor of reading I have learned many things that I did not know, and in various ways I have reserved an approach for my thoughts toward investigating greater secrets of things. Although, indeed, I am not of such great learning or industry that I would dare profess that I have grasped that secret method of the ancient sages which they used in concealing the majesty of philosophy, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not to be despised, as it seems to me, of writing altogether secretly and without any suspicion, and of concealing whatever you wish. At the urging of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince-Elector of the Roman Empire, the wisest patron of philosophers, than whom no one seemed to me more worthy, I committed these methods to writing and gathered them into the following volume, not without enormous labor.

But lest this great secret come to the ears of the unlearned or of wicked men, whoever you may be as reader, I warn, ask, and adjure you by the ineffable name of God, JEHOVAH, and by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, that you disclose this science of writing to no one unworthy, immodest, carnal, or maliciously old, since through it many things could be done among men: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, murders, and betrayals, if, which may it not happen, it were made known. For just as a good and honorable man, as often as it is necessary, can safely and without any suspicion from anyone make known and express the secret of his will to another person who knows the art, for private or common advantage, so a perverse man, immodest and blinded by carnal love, can signify to a consenting person of his desire, however shamelessly, foully, and lustfully, his evil desire, by honorable, modest, and holy words, determining the place, time, and manner of meeting, as broadly as he can, without any suspicion. Nor will there henceforth be any security among married people, while a woman can very easily understand the evil will of her lover from the best writings, with her husband looking on and praising the most holy words, without any suspicion of evil; and whatever you wish your mistress to know, however ignorant she may be of Latin words, she can send back in reply, with her husband marveling and, as is possible, carrying the message. Indeed, if this science were to come to the knowledge of the commonwealth, the whole order would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, documents, all writings, and the very conversations of men would be turned into the gravest suspicion. No one now by letters, however whenever thereafter no one would believe good, holy, and honorable men; no one would put trust in letters, however holy and chaste their words might be; it would always be thought that deceit, fraud, and evil deception lay hidden in the mouth, and men would become fearful about everything, no less suspicious of mutual conversations than of any letters whatever. But let someone object to me, saying: If you wanted this knowledge of yours to be hidden, why did you wish to commit it to writing? To him I say, if an answer must be given, that I neither ought nor could hide this knowledge from the most excellent prince, by means of which he may, if occasion arises, be able to free his dependants, of whose number I am one, from many dangers. For by means of this knowledge he can make known the conception of his mind to his own people, to whomever he wishes, secretly or openly, securely, without in the least fearing anyone's knowledge to the contrary. But whoever wishes to write anything by this art should diligently observe the methods, signs, and proportions of each thing; if he neglects to consider these, he himself will easily be able to forget what he has written. But now, with the Lord's help, let us proceed to the demonstration.

Method

The First Method of Writing Secretly is Carried Out by the Individual First Letters of Individual Words; Its Sign Is This: I.

The first, then, of the methods for writing secretly is such as this: when you wish to write something secretly to a friend, so that no one understands your intention except the one to whom you are writing, then take any Latin narrative you wish which need not be hidden, arranging all its words in such an order that the first letter of each word yields the word you wish, just as I shall teach you in the argument or example placed below. Yet this device is not sufficiently safe, because it could easily be detected by an industrious man, [unclear]. In reading, indeed, it is easy, but it is written with difficulty, because it is laborious always to have at hand words suitable to the proposition. Let us set down an example of this method, whose open text is Latin, but whose tenor, [unclear], is indicated as written in German, namely:

Example of the First Method.

[unclear]

Shining radiance of eternal blessedness, most excellent, King, governor and most mighty [unclear] of all who live virtuously, exalted and due refuge, virtue, unanimity, bond of all, joy of those who mourn, holy exultation of the sorrowful, strength of the weak, nourisher of the needy, and salvation of the afflicted, helper of the wretched, triumphator of the noble, administrator of graces, govern and rule the life of your servants, healing our infirmities, savior of all, glory of conquering souls, most brilliant light, refuge of the hungry, most kind lover of your servants, eternal rewarder of virtue, gentle glorifier of the souls serving you, [unclear] us, Lord, so that in morals

Key of Steganography

adorned with good morals, let us continually rejoice. True fortitude, strengthen us, that we may be made renewed by the brilliance of holiness. Help us, eternal God, redeemer. Free the lovers of your name; forgive sin for all; extinguish temptations for those who do harm; grant virtuous life and the love of righteousness to us as we pray, most high God, true giver of life to the weak, light of those who mourn; hear us, that we may deserve continually to maintain a just and upright life. Give us life, savior and most merciful king; be our glorifier. Zealous for truth, may we rejoice to be raised up to the eternal kingdom. Preserve the humble, pardon the new, destroy the harmful.

The Hidden Sense of the Above

Dear faithful one, you should be ready next Monday, as best you can, and wait for us around five at the Land Gate; there we shall appear with our equipment, etc. And so on, as much as you wish.

Precautions to Be Observed

But it must be observed that the aforesaid method, as we have said, is not sufficiently safe in serious matters, since as soon as any suspicion begins to arise about the letters, the secret can easily be detected by a clever person. Therefore the following methods are safer, as is clear. Likewise it must be observed, if by this or other methods you write to someone not sufficiently learned in the Latin language, that he should not divide the words, lest [unclear]. If you wish, you may use two points; I fill each word of your secret so that, when you have made a complete sentence of the outer text, you may make a little stroke thus, or the reverse, as you like. Yet it seems safer that neither points nor little strokes be made; and let the sign of a period, of whatever method, be placed not in the word of the secret, but rarely; place it neither over the first letter nor after the last, just as I did above in the hidden tenor: Dear fa[unclear]ithful one, etc.

Extension

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

Extension of This First Method

The first method itself of writing secretly, like nearly all the others, can be varied with manifold diversity, so that a person who perfectly understands the aforesaid order of concealing may still be able to perceive only with difficulty other methods to be inferred from it. For anyone can vary this method, together with the others, for his own book: namely, so that the first line is conscious of the secret, the second not; or, if it is of such size, that one is not; and so consequently the concealer of secrets, as he wishes, is alternated in alternate lines, either whole or half, by descending from the beginning of his letters to the end, or by ascending from the end to the beginning. I add also that from either side, descending and ascending [unclear] another beside the sense of his hidden [unclear] can be varied by powers so many and so diverse that, in explaining them, there is need of an Oedipus. But my present purpose is to show first the simple methods of writing, and to give to those who are worthy and suitable to know many things an occasion by which they may be able elegantly to devise the greatest things from the smallest.

The Second Method, Prudently Varied by Alternate Words, Easy and Very Safe in Every Language

The second method of writing hidden things without suspicion is that the words of the narrative of the openly proposed text be varied by alternate position: namely, so that when the first letter of the first word bears witness to the hidden intention, the first letter of the following word is free from the duty of the secret office. Afterwards the third is not free from the ministry, the fourth remains idle, and so consequently the words, mixed always in alternate turns, serve the secret, while those suited to the public discourse withdraw in prudent order from the signification of hidden things. And this method, easy in every language of the world, contains [unclear] and seems to me sufficiently safe for announcing whatever secrets you wish. Its example is as follows.

Example of the Second Method

[unclear] sweetest Jesus, extreme salvation of the blessed spirits, and [unclear] created, pardon, and hear the groans of the poor; mitigate our tribulation; renew what is old. Heal the diseases of vices; grant virtues; receive exiles; and absolve the guilty. Good Jesus, mercifully forgive any offenses of ours,

The Key of Steganography

[unclear] ours, since we have sinned gravely and have often fallen away: sweetest Savior Jesus Christ, save us; be kind to those who pray, Jesus, and preserve us, your suppliant servants. We are men, most loving Jesus, transgressing the rule of justice; mercifully rescue us, you highest virtue, since our life, continually subject to unhappiness, is corrupted. Have mercy on us, Jesus Christ, most loving Savior; look upon the humility of faithful souls, and do not permit us any longer to wander in the mire of security, of a most destructive temptation, in love, as we, badly troubled, are tossed about; led away by faults, we hold our salvation in little esteem, soon to be called to the examination of reason. Kind Creator, be gracious to your servants, and free us as quickly as possible. The vanity of the world has deceived us, for we have abandoned the way of truth; rescue the sweetest light of souls, fixed in the mire, since you are our salvation, and in your name we shall be saved: unfailing joy and everlasting happiness, you are our life, the gladness of angels, the most perfect fellowship of the just, Creator, Savior of the human race. Most kind Jesus, hear us humble ones crying to you; free us from present and future shipwreck, that we may live without end. Would that you would look upon us, your wretched servants in exile, you who have redeemed us; we have loved your ways. Preserve us, almighty God, infinite majesty, boundless compassion; be our perpetual [protection?]. Amen.

The hidden tenor of the above.

Dear faithful one, the bearer of this letter has done something wrong; it is our command that you keep him imprisoned until our arrival, etc.

Example of a Latin Secret.

The lover of human salvation, who created all things, has enjoined obedience upon us: a commandment which we all are bound to obey and follow. The reward of holy obedience will be everlasting happiness for those who fear God. Let us strive to be summoned to Christ's obedience in all things, so that we may deserve to enter the eternal life promised to us with the angels through the mercy of God. Let us do penance while we can; the time of life is very brief; soon death will strike the unprepared, suddenly it will consume the negligent. [unclear] to send souls to judgment; brothers, do not delay in doing penance, for death will come swiftly to you, which no one of you can escape for long. Look upon those passing from your [unclear]; begin penance while you have time; why do you neglect it any longer? O death, most terrible of horrible things, how swiftly you consume us wretched ones. Your sojourn is very brief, subject to judgment; death subjects all from the soul. Hear us, most loving Christ, Savior, and be gracious to us who desire [unclear] through [unclear]; grant us fear and love of you, most kind Redeemer, pardon of sins to those who supplicate you. Nourishing Creator of the human race, hear us; grant us forgiveness of crimes. O most merciful Father, be merciful to us; help our weakness, most gentle one. Thus run mercifully to the aid of our weak souls, since we are yours. Most indulgent Father, grant rest to the souls of the faithful; deign to join with the angels those who fear God.

The hidden tenor of the above.

Tonight after twelve, I shall come to you near the gate which leads to the garden, where you will wait for me. See that everything is ready.

The third method is to use alternate words in such a way that the first is always without the meaning of the secret.

The third method of secret writing, as I have said, arises from the preceding one; in it the words serving the secret are varied in alternate turns as above. Yet this must be observed: that the first word of the narrative contribute nothing to the secret intention; and, likewise, the last word of the completed sentence at the end should be without a word of the secret, together with the following word, which should precede the beginning of the next word. And this method is very safe and is not easily detected by one ignorant of the art; and we shall set down an example of this kind.

Example of the third method.

O [unclear], we die, since all of us, mortal, together bring forth the guilt of general harm, and no one lives who will not die; we are all chosen for a short time. Baptism removes original sin [in natural things?]; daily penance must be performed. Death of the body remains before us, so that in humility we may fear God, who has rescued us from sinning; we have already lost [unclear], and by preserving [it] virtuously may live again in divine light. O Jesus, [unclear] from the heavens

[unclear]

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

two valid ones following in succession. For two nulls, only at the end of the word of the mystery, completed equally by two, are placed, as will be clear.

Example of the Fourth.

[unclear]

The Passion of Jesus Christ, giving life to the human race, whose life, innocently afflicted, freed us from every calamity, because [unclear] shall be saved in necessity; but [unclear] by the vicious, and the death of the good shall be abundant. Let us speak the praise of C. J., who redeemed our souls. Therefore let us give thanks to our most pious redeemer, who redeemed all who were subject to tyranny; all have praised his blessed name, and let us do penance for our excesses. Daily we shall hasten to live virtuously in love of the redeemer, whose fear cleanses the conscience, justifying us sweetly. Let us amend our life, lamenting with devotion, so that, turned to justice, we may deserve release from sins, persevering continually in charity and humility; we shall not fail.

Joh. Trith., Abb.

The secret tenor of the above.

I still want tonight, around two, to knock at the gate; wait for me and let me in, etc., and so for the rest.

The fifth mode proceeds with the first null through two signifying ones; it concludes each thing with an alternate null.

The fifth mode, not very dissimilar to the fourth, proceeds in the customary way with the first null through two signifying words. Each word of the secret, containing one null, is always enclosed, if they are equal, by two signifying words and one null; but if the matter is among unequal ones, a solitary signifying word will stand between two nulls. Let us also set down an example of this kind.

Example of the Fifth.

One who lives justly will attain happiness; no virtue will exalt elsewhere than humility alone, unless rashness shall condemn. If you seek happiness, hold fast the love of justice; and if you desire to attain true glory, always be a zealot of truth. Do not [unclear] falsehood; it corrupts chaste honesty, temperance,

The Key of Steganography

[unclear] dispels. Flee the vanity of the world, for it is very brief. Be a lover of Jesus Christ our most merciful savior. Cultivate the virtues, flee vices, beware [unclear], and keep holy humility in your heart. Love the savior of our souls, in whose love there is abiding, everlasting life. Despise joys that will suddenly pass away; love the future eternity of blessedness promised to us. Always beware the snares of the ancient enemy, the harm of whose poison humility easily overcomes. Be watchful, lest the savagery of the crafty enemy destroy you, since he himself is always watchful, and his most impious zeal is greatly to be feared. Love God cordially; he always remains. Love of the world is quickly consumed; dread, praise, and every crowd of things are suddenly ended. Evil zeal is the way of damnation. A proud man will suffer the deadly gnawing of worms; wretched and unhappy, he will never be freed. A proud man, worst of all, will burn without interruption and will never behold the glory of eternal happiness; he is cast outside with the demons, tortured, never to be freed. Alas for us proud men, to be condemned to eternal punishment; darkness and dread will fill you. O vanity of vanities, which eternal laments follow, to be despised, for you cloud reason. Johannes Trithemius.

The Hidden Content of the Above.

On next Friday at night about one o’clock, I will be at the ditch; and when it is time to storm the castle, then seize the Westerweller, etc.

The Sixth Method, after two nulls, always takes two significatives, whether they are words or are not.

The sixth method is that, with the first two being nulls to avoid suspicion, the two following in the order of the secret signify; and if by words of equal syllables they had completed the hidden word, that word itself is, in the usual way, closed off by two idle ones; if not, until the narration falls equally through two or more mysteries, where the nulls end some hidden word, presently what follows is begun from the significatives. Let us also offer an example of this mystery.

Sixth Example.

The sum, The keys of the Steganography can all be varied with manifold diversity, according as it shall have seemed suitable to any diligent person for the concealment of his secret; but now let us set down below an example of this sort.

Seventh Example.

[unclear]

Unfailing light, blessedness of all the saints and creator [unclear], I.C. [unclear] of the universe and ruler, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and thirsting for your mercy, ask you: grant us the strength to overcome the temptations of the Devil, so that, after hard labors for you, we may deserve rest. O sweetest Savior, I pray, look upon your humble servants and useless servants; be merciful to us, since we desire with all our longings to serve you. Make us have the favor of your love always burning within us. Give us the strong bond of brotherly charity. Jesus, almighty King of heaven, make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with love for you, we may love nothing here and regard nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, most gentle Jesus, teach us to imitate your doctrine; for we are subject to various evils, intent on few goods. Save us, Lord, lest we perish. O supreme truth, give us life; sweet refuge of souls, be to us a tower of strength. For you are our strongest virtue; you are the salvation of my soul and the most healthful refreshment of my mind; you are the ineffable joy of the angels and the rest of all the faithful. You are the holy gladness of those who love you. You are the inextinguishable name of the citizens above. You are the giver of life to the dead and the most merciful sustainer of the frail. You, sweetest Jesus, help us, your frail servants, so that we may deserve to walk along the way of truth on the right path without offense. O most loving Lord Jesus, mitigate my very hard exile; and when the end of this life of mine begins to draw near, deign mercifully to come to our aid then, since [unclear], and fleeing far away all those who intend evils, they will soon be destroyed, since you are our protector. We ask by the virtue of your most noble death, sweetest one: do not despise your servants on the day of our departure, but may Jesus the Lord redeem and wash each of us with your blood, and may all [unclear] of our transgression graciously grant us, as we wait, the heavenly joys of the celestial homeland. Amen.

The hidden tenor of the above.

Dear faithful one, we have understood your business,

[unclear], very quietly, so that we may anticipate the enemy and strike them down.

The eighth method proceeds alternately by three empty words and the same number of significant words.

As the sixth does by two, so namely that any single mystical word of equal syllables completes the meaning of the open narrative in such a way that, when three empty places have been left, the following one begins not from [unclear], but from three significant words. If the word of the secret has unequal syllables, it will receive [unclear] into its company, until the syllables before the period in some way at last become equal.

Eighth example.

O almighty, eternal God, most kindly rewarder of justice, who willed your Son to become a participant in our race, that he might redeem those long placed in most wretched perdition, overflowing with goodness alone, assuming our form incorrupt from the flower of the virginal womb, as the holy Archangel Gabriel made known; which Virgin, destined to conceive by the most blessed Spirit, was to remain a virgin forever, free from crime, more eminent than all men and angels, bore the almighty King, God and man: the most holy and most reverend Virgin Mary, wholly ignorant of male companionship, giving birth without pain, and always remaining such, most high and immaculate. Holy virgin Mother of Jesus Christ, created by the power of God, known everywhere to the humble, filled with love toward other men, existing most worthy of all praise, and always remaining a virgin, [unclear] of the most blessed angels, whom then the Son admits with most generous favor in all things she has asked; and he venerates her as his most reverend mother, more excellent than all creatures, he who has never been accustomed to deny anything to one asking, but at once consents to her most holy will, granting all things, at last through the merits of this advocate of the poor. Therefore, venerating the very renowned merits of the most noble Virgin Mary, Lord Emperor of the universe, we pray that you pour the light of truth into us, wipe away the stains of sins, and truly bestow grace, especially at every time upon those who seek you; remove temptations; grant us, who beseech you, the power of conquering; clothe us with your love, chastity 18 Key of the Steganography. chastity, obedience, temperance, kindness, abstinence, and the other virtues, with the tears of all, of devout [unclear], mercifully grant to us. Amen.

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

The bearer of this letter boasts of great art; but I do not think much of it. Test him well; do not trust him. Joh. Trith.

The ninth mode begins from three vacant ones, and proceeds singly through as many significants in alternating turns.

[unclear]

The ninth mode begins from three vacant ones with the eighth, and through as many significations alternately [unclear] concludes the individual mystical words before the period with an equal syllable, that is, it is concluded by three and three through as many idle ones; but the redundant ones, if two, are ended by two, and if one, by one similar vacant letter, in such a way, if you wish, that the following mystical word is always begun with three vacant ones. Of this let us set down the following example.

The ninth example.

Greeting and affection, most beloved and most singular friend, [bearer] of the present letters and more glorious, whom I ask you to receive humanely; he will set forth to you his necessity. Since I desire, as far as I can, to relieve here his old-time necessity and the defects pressing upon him, I should wish to be able to apply consolation to his misfortunes; but since, as is clearer than daylight to you, we are exhausted by heavy losses and, as is indicated, burdened by various debts, I am strongly confident in his zeal of piety, you who hold the force and bonds of friendship, that you would willingly show yourself humane to a friend, just as you have always been accustomed to be a helper of the needs of friends. And so I ask that you lend him, for a fixed term, two hundred florins, since he is placed in the greatest necessity, as he will inform you. I trust that you will restore all things with ready integrity after he has at last been moved by you. But if you do this, I give immortal thanks; act so that we may prove your sincere love toward us in the matter. What you do for him, I would have you know, is done for me; and I shall take care to give you immortal thanks for it. The friend himself, however, Eberhard, will restore it, namely

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

[unclear], namely a loan. For he will pay what he has promised; he knows how to keep it in steadfast firmness and not to deceive. Moreover, since you enjoy hearing new reports, I shall tell you marvels. I have brought up a dog called Eris, an enemy of peasants, so skilled in learning, instruction, and memory of all things that he seems to us to have put off the beast and put on a man. He understands Greek and knows Latin words; he humbly asks pardon for offenses; whatever I order, he does, when I nod to him with gestures; he faithfully guards what is entrusted to him; he rashly discloses secrets to no one; what are both imposed and entrusted to him he [unclear]. He loves himself as a zealous defender, plays excellently, and does other things easily marvellous, not incredible to those who know them. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the above.

This man asks to borrow N. gulden from you; my advice is: leave him alone; he is utterly ruined and cannot pay.

The tenth method begins by means of four nulls, proceeds, and ends with meaningful and idle letters.

The tenth method begins from four idle letters. Through the same number of signs in order it proceeds after the likeness of the eighth in threes; that is to say, when the mystic word ends in a vowel, what follows is begun from the meaningful letters; but if it ends in meaningful letters, that is incorporated from four idle letters. But if fewer than four letters remain around the end, it can be concluded with the same number of idle letters, and also be omitted in the same number of meaningful letters. Let us set down an example of the tenth.

S.D. Since it is useful to know how to adorn a most honorable talent, and since we judge nothing more shameful to befall men than ignorance. The vanity of the world is always hostile to good and excellent talents, since it swallows a noble intellect in filth, clouds the mind, scatters memory, disturbs the senses, overthrows discipline, weakens the body, effeminates the spirit, and makes the citadel of religion and piety into woodland tales out of a man; it consumes all time in vain things, seeks the comfort of the flesh, and transgresses into destruction all the brightness of Catholic instruction; it does not revere God, it despises men, it forgets benefits, it is disturbed by the evils of conscience, it rejects eternal joys and venerates human glory, it feeds on vices, it is stained with filth and every kind of foulness,

The Key of Steganography

it thinks nothing of future things; stripped of eternal goods, it greedily loves only temporal things.

But you, best of friends, do not devote yourself to passing cares, but exalt the capacity of reasoning [unclear], and declare your intention by good morals; and, despising the world, so nobly adorn with letters your inner talent, which nature has given you, admonishing that what you show by outward possession, imitating the humble, you should truly exhibit in heart, since no one judges a gracious good to have been brought forth from a false heart; this is not said by the philosophers.

The hidden tenor of the above.

Today at one o'clock the pastor of Kirchberg has died; do not hurry so much with the handing over. Joh. Tr.

The eleventh method runs alternately through four, and concludes the word bound with meaningful letters by empty ones.

The eleventh method is always begun from four empty letters, and, proceeding alternately through the same number of meaningful letters, is ended in idle letters equal to the last meaningful letters. For all things to be concealed take their beginning from four idle letters, and however many meaningful letters you find remaining beyond four, know that so many empty letters must be appended at the end. Let an example of this be set down.

Example of the eleventh method.

S.D. I send you the oration that I delivered at the wedding of that same friend of mine: God, creator of all things, redeemer of the human race and best savior, consecrated even the use of marriage, lest the species itself perish. For we read that he also commanded marriage to the first man and said, Increase and multiply. He laid down the law for the preservation of humanity; and in the Gospel he deigned to sanctify weddings with miracles, those deserving well of God, preserving chastity. But it benefits men more who take up the modest zeal of their human state. Therefore you, who have taken up blessed wedlock according to our example and the command of the savior, who sometimes by miracles, but I by words, shall praise the institution of religion in honor of weddings. To you men, therefore, to whom we must announce weddings, and a great union of the young and religious [unclear]

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

by which the human race is preserved: for if the practice of marriage had not existed, our whole race would have fallen and perished, with no one coming to its aid. But come, you who adorn fruitful marriages: let them be venerable by right conduct, by notable examples, by the concord of peace. First of all worship God, [unclear], always spend much money in alms for the poor, live virtuously, preserve justice, love beneficence, always speak praises to God, give alms from your own. Obey the commandments of God, do not abandon truth, honor the ministers of God, pay tithes to the churches, receive pilgrims as guests, free the innocent, feed the hungry, obey your elders, honorably love your neighbors, doing injury to absolutely no one; cultivate the Christian religion most devoutly; do not follow any vain errors that have been devised. Preserve the teaching of the Gospel, and live according to the commandments of God. Despise the pleasures of the flesh, show yourselves honorable and kindly, preserve purity of heart. Loving nothing [unclear]: remember what he commanded us in the holy Gospel, C. I., saying: [unclear] when at last we preserve chastity for God amid a voluptuous life and the soul in a muddy body. Purity of heart, however, must always be nourished by honorable, humble prayer, by which the mind is purified by prayers, and prayer most powerfully removes the remedy against temptations; and therefore the holy Apostle tells you that you must always be intent upon holy prayers, lest you fail through some temptation. Let us join you in marriage, so that, by his granting, you may preserve the offspring of your race, not so that you ought to flow away in harmful pleasures [unclear] the noble dignity of substance that is to come. And so know and keep in memory that you are travelers returning to the fatherland to which you have been called; for the life of this age is brief and quickly comes to an end. Therefore live in marriage in such a way that you do not at last happen to be excluded from the kingdom of God. Farewell.

The Hidden Tenor of the Aforesaid.

We have found a great secret treasure in the earth; come quickly and help lift it out. It is fully 100,000 guilders.

The twelfth method begins its narrative with five null letters, and, proceeding alternately through the same number of significant letters, joins them, just as in the tenth we showed that it must be done through four. Let us also devise the following example of this method.

Example XII.

S.D. I had lent you my book on the deeds of the Lombards, and the volume of Bede on the times; these I ask you to send back. For it befits a wise man to be [unclear] in those things which he has promised, [unclear] of the benefits [unclear]. The injustice of dealings is twofold, namely that of unworthiness and ingratitude. Lest you [unclear] yourself to be ungrateful, since you did not keep faith with what you promised, [unclear] you most gravely with the fault of levity. Our Gracius accuses you, because, though so often asked for the loan, you rashly refused to restore it to us according to the faith promised. Farewell.

The Hidden Tenor of the Aforesaid.

Do not trust this messenger; he likes to lie.

The Thirteenth Method.

It begins its narrative with five null letters and concludes the mystic word, through the same number of significant letters, [unclear] if they were of the same letter with the eleventh. Further, if there are fewer than five letters of the mystery, or if any remain after five, they must be concluded with as many null letters as the significant letters that immediately preceded them in number; but the mystic word, however many significant letters it has, is nevertheless begun from five null letters. Let us also devise the following example of this method.

Example XIII.

S.D. The greatest glory of nobles is philosophy, making ignorance a disgrace and the cause of all evils. For what is more beautiful than that men are found to have acted by letters and virtues, not only to attack barbarians with arms but also with learning, and, reporting the memory of their deeds, entrusted it to posterity? Yet, stirred by their example, you do not cease to unfold letters of humanity and the good arts, strenuous in arms, in study, thus all the ancients

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

Princes have most wisely been accustomed not to shut up riches to be kept in treasuries, but to apply them to the use of letters, judging this the most honorable path for those tending toward happiness: the benefit of letters, by which the commonwealth is made immortal. For indeed the knowledge of writings from [unclear] is called the burial of the living. It brings ignominious calamity upon human beings and makes them like beasts; true nobility, by contrast, is accustomed to make the soul splendid with learning and virtues. Infinite is the fruit of letters, which wins glory and holiness for our souls in heaven and shows itself immortal to those born of earth. Add that love of writing, since it extinguishes the fires of the flesh, harmful to the spirit, alone conferred on those ancient philosophers the finest memory and immortality of name among all posterity, always enclosed as venerable to human beings. Philosophy also makes those devoted to the studies of the ancestors glorious and splendid, lovers of tranquility, just, gentle, conquerors of the passions of the soul, most steadfast despisers of luxury and baseness. For these there is an easy ascent to God; holy exercises are an example of honorableness and a rule for every virtue; it shines forth in contemplation of heavenly things, sweetly raised up. They attain divine illumination, dear to God in honor, reverenced by men. Imitate these things, devote yourself to letters, confirm the happiness of life by upright works. Farewell. I, Johannes Trithemius, abbot, have written this.

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

Those of Nuremberg have sent scouts out against you / in many forms / look out for yourself / etc.

Mode XIV. Between two nulls it encloses each mystical word with its signifying words.

Mode 14 always takes its beginning from a null and, duly proceeding in order through signifying matter by means of one null, encloses at the end the word to be hidden. Moreover, students in this art will be able not only to vary but also to enlarge the preceding thirteen modes, so that, beginning with those things at the various number where we ended the demonstration, they may ascend, up to whatever number they wish, by 7, 8, 9, 10, or more alternately, wherever they wish.

Example

24 Key of Steganography. Example XIV.

Apply yourself to letters with humble submission; be kind; most diligently beware ignorance. For teaching, celebrated by training, exalted in honorableness, learning distinguished by morals, is to be preferred to all honors. Knowledge immersed in vices has little worth, but diligent learning always makes a noble life, marked by virtues and adorned with examples of learning; adorned innocence is given esteem, since heavenly honor must be preserved by holy actions. Unfruitful knowledge will be subject to torments, but in elevated sciences friendly letters [unclear] with living virtues, and pleasures that are stained and to be overthrown; one must insist on exercises of virtues, or sweetnesses must be granted. Farewell from Sponheim, 7 Kalends of January, in the year of Christ 1498. Johannes Trithemius.

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

I ask you, let me know how the matter stands, as you well know.

Mode XV. It begins from the unit that marks, and proceeds alternately up to the number eight.

Mode 15 sets one idle word before, adds another signifying word, then two alternates, three follow, and so up to eight; moreover from the group of eight through seven, then through six, and so consequently down to the unit, the descent is again made; and again, in the same way, ascent and descent to the unit, as often as will be necessary.

Example XV.

Most illustrious Prince, with humble subjection, greeting. Princes must rightly be instructed in good disciplines and with virtues and learning, and should justly hold and knowingly govern the commonwealth. For the most glorious authority of leaders is to apply themselves at once to arms and letters: to destroy the enemy in war, and by the arts of letters to adorn the mind, and to rule with courage and wisdom together. God, the most excellent illuminator of all hearts, has bestowed noble knowledge upon us, which I shall, to the best of my powers, care for by your grace. For it has a distinguished, bright ministry of understa-

John Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim

[unclear] that all things are rightly to be hidden from human understanding, namely lest, by using them badly, they be subverted. You understand well enough that the secret of the divine art is to be revealed to benevolent princes, chaste, just, learned, and worthy men, so that they may be able to beware cunningly of men’s very grave errors, evil counsels, and the snares of the wicked, and may have power to disturb the efforts of enemies, who zealously disturb the commonwealth, and [unclear] in protecting affairs he may send letters securely in silence. Therefore, dearest and most honorable prince, since I, a man who loves knowledge, have known by kindness [unclear] to favor the best arts, I strove to present this knowledge, hidden from all, as clear to the sole [unclear], most beloved, who by great virtues surpasses all nobles, kings, and princes of our time [unclear], outstanding in religion, liberality, justice, and consequently in nobility, and admirable and conspicuous in literary learning. God has given us the grace of understanding; he has set forth various arts not uselessly. But [unclear] to carry out the matter with zeal and to apply ourselves to holy impulses, so that we may deserve to enter the happiness of life appointed for us after death; and knowledge will be a support to us. Amen. Farewell.

The hidden content of the aforesaid.

I beg your Grace: keep the art secret until the book is made; I have found still wondrous things for it.

Mode XVI. It agrees with the preceding mode in its procedure, but, on the contrary, always begins from the vacant words.

The third mode is opposed to the preceding one as regards the beginning, because that one begins its first narrative from significant words. This one, however, begins from idle words, so that the first word is always empty, but the second significant; and so an ascent is made from unity up to the octave, from which again there is a descent down to unity, and this as often as the proposed narrative is finished. Let us fashion the following example of this kind.

Example XVI.

One ascends to eternal life by virtues alone, since those given over to vices have by no means been judged worthy of the kingdom of God, and their pride has been repelled; they are zealous for the iniquity of demons, and they will always be disturbed by zeal [unclear], and the worms of impiety will gnaw them. Their consciences will never rest for eternity, but, blinded, they will be punished with the greatest torments, with everlasting oblivion. In hell there is no redemption, but perpetual weeping and unceasing groaning and a fire never to be extinguished. There are darkness and everlasting night, fear and very grievous misery, cold and chill; there will be no degree, for always to lack perpetual goods, to endure burning or cold or [zeal?], which is blameworthy. For carnal pleasure is very brief; in exchange for its object, wretched men are increased by the greatest miseries, [unclear]; but the salvation of our people remains continually [unclear]. Farewell.

The hidden content of the aforesaid.

When this man comes to you, put him in prison until my arrival, etc. And so with the rest as much as one pleases.

Mode XVII. It imitates the first mode through the individual words, the letters always being in the preceding one.

The seventeenth mode, after the pattern of the first, begins with the first letters through the individual words, but arranges the letters of the alphabet artfully, so that for a it takes b, for b it takes c, and so consequently up to the end of the alphabet; moreover, for z it takes A. And when you wish to write in such a mode, so that you may the more easily be able to follow the alphabet, consider its order by nature.

A b c d e f g h k l m n o p q r s t u x z.

b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q R S T U X Z A.

For A, b, the immediately following letter, is taken; for B, C; for D, D [unclear]; and so consequently, as is clear in the example.

Example XVII.

The majesty of the catholic [faith?], firmer than all things by holy deeds, has promised, with Christ’s favor, the happiness of eternal life to faithful men who hold the catholic faith. Christ, the more glorious almighty, bestows future life; no one of wicked works will have blessed life. A faithful man follows Christ by holding to virtue; he is declared by good works, and the catholic name of Christia-

28. The Key of Steganography.

The hidden tenor of the above: [German] "Peter Kleipfeyel, the bearer of this letter, is a wicked rogue, full [drunk] day and night, a despiser of the name of God."

Modus XIX: after each single vacant [letter] it sets two significant [letters], with the letters transposed in the aforesaid manner. Modus 19: you premise one vacant [letter], to which it always subjoins two significant [letters] with the letters transposed at pleasure, so that always after one idle, transposed [letter], two significant and transposed [letters] follow. And this transposition can be varied as if to infinity, as we shall say in what follows; and of this modus let us set down the following example, in which we shall observe the transposition of letters said above, so that in place of any letter the one always immediately following it be taken.

Example XIX. [Latin cover-text, a moralizing passage on the catholic faith, as printed.]

The hidden tenor of the above: [German] "Dear faithful one, today about ten [o'clock] await us with four hundred horse at the gate."

Modus XX: with the letters of the significant [words] transposed, after each two vacant [letters] it sets as many significant. Modus 20: after two idle [letters] placed at the beginning, set always two significant [letters] with the letters transposed, in the same manner we said—namely, that for each [letter] the next immediately following be taken; but the empty words in the narration do not transpose a letter, as is said above—at least, if you wish; and of this [modus] too, in turn, let us set down the following example.

Example XX.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

adorned, furnished us with every idea and material for disputing, approaching fervently and vigorously with the most holy devotion of mind in the religion of piety. What, I ask you, [unclear] in a religious community, where Catholic conduct flourishes, where nothing idle is said, nothing wicked is hidden. May Christ Jesus, savior of all, cause us to rejoice in heavenly glory, and may the love and fervor of God refresh all true zealots of truth. We have rejoiced with holy joy, praying and beseeching that you receive the brother calmly, and lay aside every zeal of bitterness. Farewell, from Sponheim, on the Nones of January, in the year 1598. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.

Mode XXIX. It uses alternate words, and the first letter of each significant word is shifted to the tenth.

Mode 29 similarly uses alternate words, like the preceding modes, beginning with one empty word, to which another significant one is soon joined; again one empty word, and again one significant word, and so consequently to the end of the proposed narrative. But the first letter of each significant word is shifted to the eleventh following, so that for A, l is taken; for b, m; for c, n; and so consequently, as is clear in the alphabet itself.

A, b, m, c, n, a o, e p, f q g r h i k u x z na ob pc qd re ss g t g u h xi zk.

Content of the Secret.

Beware of the bearer of this letter; he is a bad knave. Do not trust him at all; he is deceiving you. I know him very well.

Significant Letters.

Example XXIX.

SD. Since you are most devoted to the arts of humane learning, I think you will surely rejoice that you have found a ninth companion of your studies. This man, who presents these letters to you, is a man of much knowledge, a supreme philosopher, a most subtle arithmetician, a most eloquent rhetorician, a most profound mathematician, and excellently learned in every [unclear]. He speaks most elegantly, shining with Ciceronian eloquence. Were I not so much your friend, I would have kept such a man entirely for myself, since, having enjoyed his familiar company, I have found him to be most learned among philosophers. I am especially favorable to you, that you may receive so gratefully so great a philosopher, whom, led by singular friendship toward you, I send to you; and by showing yourself benevolent and familiar to him, you will prove him a supreme philosopher. I have seen certain secrets of the arts committed to most elegant letters, by which they accomplish wonders. This most learned man can answer ex tempore the very weighty questions proposed to him; in proposing, he uses a zeal most ready for disputation. Therefore I ask that you receive him liberally and humanely, a man most learned in all good arts by culture and familiarity, and a very weighty defender. Indeed, he will be able to instruct you in many things, since he is a philosopher of most elegant learning, an outstanding historian, a most skilled rhetorician too, ready, and a most acute geometer. O would that all our students were such, who with swollen breast despise necessary study. But this man, devoted to philosophy, and other sciences and arts, loves them deeply, treats them continually, and penetrates them most acutely. Receive him therefore with love; treat him with a generous countenance; strengthen the faithful Christian. Farewell, from Sponheim, on the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1499. Johannes Trithemius.

Mode XXX. It proceeds by alternate words, and the significant letter is shifted to the eleventh.

Mode 30, beginning with one empty word, proceeds by alternate words, so that throughout the whole sequence of the narrative it always places after one empty word another significant word, just as we have shown in the preceding mode also and in others. Moreover, by the fourth letter of the significant word the first following after it is taken as the eleventh, so that for A, m is taken; for b, n; for c, o; and so consequently, as is clear in the alphabet.

Am, bn, eo, dp, eq, fr, gs, ht, iu, kx, wz, ma, nb, oc, pd, qe, rs, sgth, ni, xk, zl.

Content of the Secret.

They have written to me that I should come to him, but I am not coming; you must first write to me beforehand.

Letters

30. Key of Steganography. Method XXI. It uses alternating significant words, with the letters transposed into the second place.

Method 21 uses alternating words, of which the first is empty, the second indeed significant, the third again empty, the fourth by no means idle; and so on in succession down to the end of the proposed narrative. All the letters in the significant word are transposed into the second following place, so that for the letter A, c is to be taken; for c, e is to be taken; and so on in succession to the end of the alphabet. Further, for x, a is to be taken, but for z, b. The Greek y, however, is not necessary for us for an ordinary name, and therefore is to be omitted in all the following alphabets. But now let us set down an example of this kind.

Example XXI.

I should rejoice to answer your letters; so may Christ make me rejoice, and I would send the requested volumes, if at last I had had them. I have been zealous, I think, for my nearest and most serious hidden handlers lately with a good zeal, as the most exact philosophers had it; moreover I shall have for you thanks far from mortal, my sweetest brother, you who keep mutual glory inviolate. For in this familiar matter, which you seem to have attended to most diligently with grave modesty, I have plainly learned this: that I praise what has been done and shall have thanks that will never die. And therefore, complying with your requests, I should soon have wished to be, Christ knows, the things requested, if I had them. Here I have nowhere seen a Latin translation of Master Ficino; I confess I have read at Venice the beloved letter of Pico della Mirandola. Therefore do not take it hard that your petitions are so frustrated. The highest truth of your Christ conceals nothing in darkness, and, as examiner of hearts, that I could not oblige you. To hide the other best things, to scorn virtue and very many gains swiftly, at last you think true, to love Christ purely. I ask, see to it that you exist as a priest in works, and that the lover of Christ more truly love Christ purely, whom you are commanded to fear. He is preserved by zeal for souls, and sets nothing before Christ's commands, since he knows that the fear of God is the best zeal of the soul, the love of blessedness, God zealous by loving. For the true royal knowledge of the Savior, and the pious observance of the catholic faith, and increasing thanks to almighty God Jesus Christ, the more glorious giver of all good things, may confer on you loves of eternity, and inscribe you in the catalogue of faithful Christians. Farewell.

Tenor [unclear]

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

31

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

Peter, printer of Fridburg, called Labsodel, likes to drink strong wine. He has been made Doctor of Fools at Sponheim.

Method XXII. With the transposition of letters already mentioned preserved, after two idle words he sets down the same number of significant ones.

Method 22 begins with idle things and at once adds two significant ones, and so, by means of two empty words and two significant words, it completes the whole open and hidden narrative in alternating turns. The first letters of all the significant words are placed in the third position, so that for a, d is to be taken; for b, e is to be taken; but for c, f; and so on in succession to the end, just as for the first letter of the alphabet A, x is to be taken; for b, [unclear]; and for z, c, as in secret matters the alphabet showing [unclear] their red visited black, hidden this time.

A d b c e f g h i k l m k p q r s x t z n a x ss z c.

But when you wish to write in the prescribed manner that follows, set the alphabet before you, and look carefully that you keep the prescribed order, lest you cause error for the reader and for yourself. But now let us set down an example, which proceeds by two alternating words.

Example XXII.

S D. Since I have known you to be a lover of the arts of humanity and of the devoted, and a cultivator of the Christian faith and the most benevolent patron of all philosophers, willingly, led by the wonderful pleasure of friendship, to oblige your requests, from books well known about ecclesiastical writers and catholic doctors, [unclear] for you to be exhorted, behold, I send it, so that you may have something with which to offend the mind. May you send back to me the codex from torments into books of foolishness concerning spirits, and the glorious work of [unclear] coming, which you have shuddered at in questions. I beseech Christ to adorn the eyes of our heart with the most holy zeal of his love, and to make us, freed from love of heavenly goods and from lowest desires, [unclear] to despise vain honors, so that in turn the lofty and also great secrets of the art may penetrate

32 Key of Steganography

that we may penetrate [unclear], and [unclear] a continual desire for glory, with the duty purified, whereby we may always adorn the Catholic faith with most honorable morals; by the virtue of humility may we become better every day, despise transitory things, and not seek to please men. You are a great and truer philosopher: let go of all things and you will find all things; and the discovery nearest to death, insofar as it offends the erring man. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

What I have given you to keep, you shall preserve and give to no one except to me alone.

Mode XXIII. With each letter shifted to the fourth, it proceeds by alternating turns or words.

Mode 23 always begins with one idle word, to which it immediately joins one significant word, and so proceeds with alternating words. In the meaning of these, the first letters are always transposed to the fourth, so that for a, e is taken; for b, f; for c, g; and so consequently as far as x, for which c is taken, as in the following alphabet we shall clearly show by example.

A e, b f, c g, d h, e i, s k, h l, i k, o l, p m, q n, r o, s p, d q, u l, r x, s z, t a, s b, x c, z d.

This mode, however, like all the others, will be capable of being varied in many ways: as it now uses alternate words, so let it use pairs, threes, or more. Then the sign of a mode of this kind is to be sought; and it must always be observed immovably for the others, since one should look not to the variety of the mode but to the order of the mystery.

Example XXIII.

S. D. Those matters which I set before myself to be solved, with Christ’s help I have resolved. I would like you to write back to me briefly what you make of it, what then has benefited me, your opinion, and the whole matter. Brother Gratius, and also a friend, recently reported to me that then, among our people, a young man had been restored to life, recounting every invocation of Christ from the dead, and telling of the wondrous and dreadful torments among the lower regions of wicked Christians: namely, of those who, by acting perversely, crucified Christ; those especially guilty who, though they had obtained the most kindly benefit of redemption, nevertheless always remained ungrateful to Christ and, utterly blinded, neglected future joys. Following the pleasures of the world, they were most bitterly [unclear] with daily and continual neglects gnawing at them: “We shall be condemned; we are justly tortured; deservedly do we suffer cruel things. Cruel as we are, we sought earthly and worldly things ambitiously; we neglected Christ’s commandment; we despised the humble; we loved iniquity; and we receive the repayment of eternal damnation. Alas for us unhappy ones, why did we deny Christ, why did we neglect the time of indulgence?” etc. The man raised up related that he had found many other wondrous things, etc. I cannot write them on this occasion, especially in a few letters. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

Tomorrow at nine o’clock take heed of me at the gate. There I will appear secretly and silently with 200 horses.

Mode XXIV. It takes all significant words, and transposes each letter to the fifth following.

Mode 24, after the likeness of the first, takes all the words of the proposed narrative as significant; but it transposes the first letter of each word to the fifth next following: that is to say, so that for a, f is taken; for b, g; for c, h; and so consequently, as we shall show in the second alphabet, where for the red letter the black one immediately placed above it is taken.

A f, b g, c h, d i, e k, f l, g m, h n, i o, k p, l q, r u, x z, s t, b v, c x, d z, e [unclear].

Therefore, whenever you wish to write or read in this mode, place this alphabet before you, easily indicating all the signs of each mode.

Example XXIV.

S. D. Setting the honor of benefactions before attentive services, and not provoking the insults of benefactors, remember, I beseech you, the holy charity of your brothers, the good zeal and honor of those brothers of yours who continually adorn our Catholic religion with holy works. But I pray, kind brother, that I may cast away fear. Double-tongued brothers, the hatred of being loved, quarrels, and disputes take goodness away by evil works. Be splendid every day to the good also; aspire also to fame; adorn the soul with holiness, justice, continence; and have zeal for the name [unclear].

34 Key of Steganography

of your name: Zelato, the most honorable and best name of friends and brothers, [unclear], a name [unclear] by just works; chastity of body also adorned, as is wont to happen with Catholic morals. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

Do not heed my word; I do not mean it so harshly; it must now be so; I will tell you the reason.

Mode XXV. Like the preceding, it admits all significant words, but transposes each to the sixth.

Mode 25, like the preceding, admits no empty word, but all the words which it admits are significant, because there is no need to insert any idle words, since there is no one in this world who, without the art of this book, could discover the secret knowledge written in these modes. Nevertheless, whoever, for greater caution or for ease, wishes to insert alternately, or after two or more empty words, the same number of significant words, we do not forbid it, especially since we know the letter for each person, so that he may, at his own pleasure, either invent new ones, if he can, or alter these as he wishes. Yet we advise them not to neglect to put the signs of the modes in their proper place, lest he himself cause others to err, as we have done, if he writes in this mode; because in each one, and in this twenty-fifth, the letters are transposed to the following sixth, as we shall show in its place. There follow the twenty-five modes of the alphabet mentioned above, in which for A let g be taken, because it is the sixth after a; for b, c; i, d; k, e; l, f; m, g; n, h; o, i; p, k; q, t; r, m; s, n; t, o; u, p; x, q; z, r; a, s; b, t; c, a; d, x; e, z; f.

When, therefore, you wish to write something either in this mode or in the other modes, once the alphabet arranged for this purpose has been set before you, put the first significant letters, written on one sheet, before you, as we do below for an example.
